full_judgment:
Md Ali Reza, J: Plaintiffs have preferred this revision calling upon the opposite party 1 to show cause as to why the judgment and order dated 8-1-2019 passed by the Joint District Judge, Court No.2, Gazipur in Title Suit 103 of 2010 allowing the application under section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure should not be set-aside and/or such other or further order or orders passed to this court may seem fit and proper.
2. The petitioners as plaintiffs filed Title Suit 103 of 2010 on 26-5-2010 in the Court of Joint District Judge, Court No.2, Gazipur against as many as 310 defendants and the suit was filed for partition. The land is 22.77 acres out of which plaintiffs claimed 500.59 decimals of land from CS Khatian 32 corresponding to SA Khatians 27, 70, 71, 73, 74, 75, 76, 77, 78, 97, 72 and RS Khatians 83, 74, 72, 58, 17, 53, 48, 24, 14, 8 and 6. In the suit, the Government is also one of the defendant being co-sharer on the basis of Land Acquisition Case 41 of 1961-62.
3. Opposite party 1, who is defendant 30 in the suit. He filed written statements on 23-3-2015 and stated that the suit is not maintainable and the same is barred under section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. He further stated in his written statement that the predecessor of the plaintiffs earlier filed Title Suit 284 of 1969 for partition which was subsequently renumbered as Title Suit 96 of 1970 and also 65 of 1974. Subsequently, the suit was transferred to the Court of Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Gazipur and renumbered as Title Suit 627 of 1985. In which the plaintiffs by practicing fraud upon the Court obtained final decree ex-parte on 12-5-1986.
4. Against which the defendants 2 and 3 of that suit filed Miscellaneous Case 164 of 1985 under Order 9 r.13 and the original suit was restored. Later on the plaintiffs again manage to obtain a preliminary and final decree by fraudulent means on 10-8-1985. Although by the subsequent order dated 5-12-1985 the earlier decree was set-aside and suit was restored to its original number. It is further stated that the preliminary and final decree since were set-aside the Title Suit 627 of 1985 was restored and subsequently it was renumbered Title Suit 99 of 2003 and ultimately the earlier 99 of 2003 was dismissed upon rejection of the plaint on 22-11-2023. Plaintiffs took fraudulent means in conducting the earlier Title Suit 627 of 1985 and the present suit was filed by suppressing all the earlier facts which tantamount to fraud and the present suit was not maintainable.
5. The opposite party 1 then filed an application for rejection of the plaint on ground of res-judicata under section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. That application he stated that the predecessor of the present plaintiffs Farid Khan along with 3 others filed Title Suit 284 of 1969 impleading same of the defendants of the present suit. The suit was ultimately renumbered as Title Suit 627 of 1985 and plaintiffs entered into a compromise with some of the defendants on 10-8-1985 and according to that compromise preliminary decree was passed and the Commissioner's report was filed on 10-4-1986. Since nobody raised any objection against that Commissioner's report. The report was accepted and the compromise decree was mate final on 12-5-1986 and parties to the compromise got possession on 7-6-1987 through decree Execution Case 4 of 1987. Now since plaintiffs filed the instant suit in respect of the same property against the same parties. This suit cannot run because it is barred by res-judicata.
6. The trial Court allowed the application of defendant 30 by judgment and order dated 8-1-2019 on the finding that since final decree was passed on the basis of compromise between the parties. The present suit between same parties with respect to the same property is not maintainable under section 11 of the Code. The Court further found that since all the disputes of title have been finally decided by the Court, this Court cannot entertain the suit again being barred under the provisions of law.
7. Against which the plaintiffs have come before this Court with this revision.
8. Mr Md Khurshedul Alam, learned Advocate for the petitioners submits that plea of res-judicata can be decided by adducing evidence after framing of issue. But the learned Court without considering the same allowed the application thus committed error of law resulting in an error in such order occasioning failure of justice. He then refers Annexure-D which is a suit registered and also a permanent document and submits that this Annexure-D shows the suit was ultimately renumbered as Title Suit 99 of 2003 and there are as many as 75 defendants in the suit and the suit finally ended when the plaint was rejected on 22-11-2003. Actually there was no issue framed in the suit and the matter in issue and the subject matter of the suit were not finally decided in that suit. Moreover, this Annexure-D finds strong support from the statement made by defendant 30 now opposite party 1 in his written statement. Thus it appears that the contention of the defendants is definitely not correct and the trial Court failed to appreciate these aspects of the case and had this statement being looked into by the trial Court the result of the case would have been otherwise. The trial Court did not notice the ultimate result of this case and passed this erroneous order thus committed error of law occasioning failure of justice in allowing the application for rejection of the plaint upon fanciful consideration. In support of his submission he refers to the case of Md Shahjahan Siraj vs Md Rafique Quoraishi and others, 19 BLC (AD) 143; Sreemati Push pa Rani Das and another vs AKM Habibur Rahman and others, 1993 BLD (AD) 217; Md Mahbubul Hague vs Md A. Kader Munshi, 2000 BLD (AD) 82 = 52 DLR (AD) 49 and State of Maharashtra and another vs M/s. National Construction Company, Bombay and another, AIR 1996 SC 2367 and finally submits question of res-judicata cannot be decided from a reading of the plaint and should be decided at the time of trial after framing and issue to that effect.
9. Mr Md Alal Uddin, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party 1 submits that the Court below did not commit any error of law resulting in an error in such order and considering the facts and circumstances of the instant case, the order was correctly passed and this Court has got nothing to interfere with that decision. He further submits that the suit is barred by res-judicata and the cause of action of the suit is absolutely false and the trial Court correctly pass the order and the Rule is liable to be discharged. Since the predecessor of the plaintiffs entered into a compromise in the earlier suit, this subsequent suit filed as his instance is barred by res-judicata. Even the petitioners of this revision obtained this Rule by misleading this Court on ground of condonation of delay and the statements made in the application for condonation of delay is absolutely false because the certified copy were taken on such a date which is otherwise mentioned in the application.
10. Mr Kazi Akhter Hosain, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of opposite parties 138, 140 and 141 submits that both the suits were partition suits and in both the suits parties are also same and the property is also identical and it is also admitted by the plaintiffs that the suit actually was disposed of on compromise. So this subsequent suit filed by the plaintiffs or their defendants is hit by section 11 of the Code. This suit cannot be adjudicated by a competent Court of law because in such event under section 11 of the Code shall be come redounded. He very candidly submits that the earlier suit having being disposed of by deciding the maters in issue substantially between the parties, the present suit is not maintainable. In support of his submission he refers to the case of Rasheda Begum vs MM Nurussafa and others, 9 MLR (AD) 294 = 9 BLC (AD) 223 and Syed Md Shah fatal Nure Alam and others vs Salimullah Chowdhury and others, 10 MLR (AD) 90 and concludes his submission as it is the schedule principal of law that subsequent suit between the same parties and in respect of same issues arising out of the same property decided in previous suit is barred by the principals of res-judicata as provided under section 11 of the Code and thus he prays that the Rule might be discharged.
11. Mr Md Asraful Islam, learned Advocate appearing for opposite party 2 opposed the Rule and adopted the submissions made by the learned Advocate for opposite parties 138, 140 and 141. He also prays for discharging the Rule.
12. We have heard the learned Advocates of both the sides, perused the revisional application and the counter affidavit filed by the opposite parties and also gone through the impugned judgment and decisions preferred to us by the parties.
13. It is contented by the petitioners that defendant 30 now opposite party 1 filed an application on 20-6-2018 in the Court of Joint District Judge, Court No.2, Gazipur for rejection of the plaint under order 11 of the Code. In which defendant 30 made out a case that the father of the present plaintiffs along with 3 others as plaintiffs filed Title Suit 284 of 1969 against some of the defendants of the present suit and the suit ultimately renumbered as Title Suit 99 of 2003 on 22-11-2003 and at that stage the plaint of the suit was rejected. Thus it appears the suit never ended on merit and since the same was not finally decided the learned Court committer error of law resulting occasioning failure of justice. He filed Annexure-D which is the suit register of that particular suit and the suit register shows that Title Suit 284 of 1969 in the year of 1969 which was later on renumbered as Title Suit 26 of 1985 has ultimately being named as Title Suit 99 of 2003 whose plaint was rejected on 22-11-2003.
<u>14. It also appears from reading of paragraph 19(Tha) of the written statement filed by opposite party No.1 that the case of the petitioners with respect to Annexure-D is clearly supported by defendant 30. The written statement was filed on 23-3-2015 but the application for rejection of the plaint on ground of res judicata was filed on 28-6-2018. So it explosively transfers that defendant 30 has filed this application for rejection of the plaint upon deliberate misrepresentation because it is clear that he had sufficient knowledge about the fake and result of the earlier suit as has been disclosed in his written statement. The counter affidavit filed by defendant 30 also does not oppose such statement with any explanation. So it is clear that the earlier suit was not disposed of finally on merit. Question of bar of res-judicata involves determination of facts and law necessitating investigation without which a plaint under the law should not be rejected. Question of res-judicata is mix questions of law and fact which required evidence to be lead by both the parties. Clause 11(d) of Order 7 is not available for rejection of plaint on the plea of res-judicata from a reading of the plaint and the question can be reserved at the trial Court after framing an issue. It is only when an issue is finally decided that it operates as res-judicata in a subsequent suit. In the instant suit the final decree was passed upon compromise with some of the defendants leaving aside the title of the other defendants undecided. It is one of the spirits of section 11 is that a matter which though in issue was not heard and decided either actually or constructively cannot be res-judicata for the purpose of subsequent proceedings. It is true though in some cases it has been held that a decision in a consent decree may operate as res-judicata, a compromise decree is not a decision by the Court. It is an acceptance of something to which the parties agreed. The compromise decree merely sets the seal of the Court on the agreement of the parties and section 1.1 is not applicable to such a decree. It is now law is must develop and it has now become ... that question of res-judicata can be decided from a reading of the plaint and cannot be decided from a reading of the plaint and should be decided at the time of trial. Moreover, in the instant case the Government is also made party as defendant 268 by virtue of Land Acquisition Case 41 of 1961-62. The matter in issue in this suit is not directly and substantially is not the issue between the same parties and no such issue was framed and has been heard and finally decided by such Court, so question of res-judicata does not arise at all and since once defendant 30 who actually started this allegation of res-judicata, although admitted in his written statement that the earlier suit ended because the plaint was rejected but by misleading the Court and false representation made out this false case of rejection of the plaint which cannot be sustained in accordance with law. We do not find any semblance of the facts and circumstances of the cases referred by the opposite parties with the present case. Thereafter, we are inclined to hold that the ratio laid down in those cases is not applicable in the present case because the reading of decisions of 19 MLR and 10 MLR cases. It appears that the earlier suits were disposed of on merit for which the subsequent suits statements as has been held by our Appellate Division were correctly barred by res-judicata.</u>
15. We also find relevant of the cases referred by learned Advocate for the petitioners in support of his case and we have also gone through those decisions and we have no hesitation to accept the ratio laid down in those cases.
16. We therefore find merit in this Rule. Accordingly, the Rule is made absolute. The impugned judgment passed by the Court is hereby set-aside. Title Suit 103 of 2010 now pending before the Joint District Judge, Court No.2, Gazipur shall proceed in accordance with law.
Communicate this judgment to the concerned Court.
End.

full_judgment:
Md Atabullah, J: This Rule Nisi was issued at the instance of the petitioner Lamashempur A timer Jame Mosque, calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the Notice bearing Memo No. 31-3-0000.031.33.668.13-48/2(1) dated 17-2-2016 issued by the respondent No. 3, Zonal Settlement Officer, Sylhet, in Miscellaneous Case No. 846 of 2016 filed under rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 should not be declared to have been issued without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may deem fit and proper.
2. Short facts, relevant for the purpose of disposal of the Rule, are that 59 decimals of land appertaining to SA Plot No. 209 under SA khatian No. 113, JL No. 323, Lamashempur, Gowainghat, Sylhet belonged to the predecessors of the SA recorded tenant Mosrab Ali who orally gifted the said land to the petitioner Lamashempur Jame Mosque of whose Motwalli is Hafiz Nazrul Islam, successor of Mosrab Ali. The Mosque Committee has been possessing the land by constructing a Mosque thereon and connecting electricity line and paying electricity bill regularly on behalf of the said mosque. But the draft RoR was prepared neither in the name of the petitioner nor in the name of the respondent No. 4. The respondent No. 4, Lamashempur Purbotul Jame Mosque represented by Motwalli Abdul Musabbir filed Objection Case No. 399 before the Settlement Officer under rule 30 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 which was allowed on 27-4-2009 in absence of the petitioner and draft record-of-right was prepared in the name of the respondent No. 4, Lamashempur Purbotull Jame Mosque.
3. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the said order dated 27-4-2009 the petitioner preferred an appeal being No. 13274 of 2015 under rule 31 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 before the Zonal Settlement Officer, Sylhet which was transferred to Assistant Settlement Officer (Appeal Officer), Jaintapur, Sylhet who upon hearing both the sides by an order dated 18-1-2016 allowed the appeal setting aside the order dated 27-4-2009 passed in Objection Case No. 399 and draft record-of-right was prepared in the name of the petitioner Lamashempur Atimer Jame Mosque, Jaintapur, Sylhet.
4. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the order dated 18-1-2016 passed in Appeal No. 13274 of 2015, the respondent No. 4 filed Miscellaneous Case No. 846 of 2016 under rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 before the Zonal Settlement Officer, Sylhet who issued a notice to the petitioner by Memo No. 31-3- 0000.031.668.13-47 / 2(1) dated 17-2-2016 for hearing the said Miscellaneous Case No. 846 of 2016 against which the petitioner filed this writ petition and obtained the present Rule.
5. Mr Khairul Alam, learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that, the petitioner Lamashempur Atimer Jame Mosque is the owner and possessor of the land in dispute which was not recorded in the draft khatian in the name of petitioner for which the petitioner filed an appeal being No. 13274 of 2015 under rule 31 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 and obtained an order on contest. He also submits that where there is no specific allegation of fraud in the elements of fraud in the whole proceeding, no question of review lies since the settlement authority has got no jurisdiction to reopen the matter other than to send the draft publication khatian for final publication under rule 32 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 and even the said rule 42A does not empower the Settlement Officer to sit and act as an appellate authority over an appellate order passed under rule 31 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 and, as such, the petition filed under rule 42A is not entertainable rather it is liable to be rejected. He relied upon the decision passed in the case of Zahirul Islam vs Government of Bangladesh reported in 65 DLR 168.
6. Mr M. Khaled Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent No. 4 submits the settlement officer has been vested with the powers to discharge function under rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 and may make correction of fraudulent entry since the draft record-of-rights has not yet been finally published. He also submits that there is no illegality in the issuance of the notice to the petitioner and mere issuance of notice would not cause any grievance to file a writ petition. He further adds that the Appeal Officer without obtaining authorization from the Settlement Officer illegally heard and allowed the appeal No. 13274 of 2015 under rule 31 condoning a long period of delay and, as such, the Appeal Officer committed fraudulent act in allowing the appeal under rule 31 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955. He relied upon the decisions passed in the cases of Mainuddin Ahammed vs the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh and others reported in 7 SCOB (2016) HCD 134 and Rawson Ara Khatun @ Rawson Ara Begum vs Government of Bangladesh and others reported in 26 BLC (AD) 12.
7. Mr Tushar Kanti Roy, learned Deputy Attorney-General appearing for the respondent Nos. 1-3 submits that under rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 the settlement officer has been vested with the power to discharge functions under the rule 42A and may make correction of fraudulent entry before final publication of record-of-rights and he committed no error of law and illegality in issuing the notice to the petitioner.
8. We have perused the materials on record meticulously. It appears from the record that the respondent No. 4 appeared in the appeal filed under rule 31 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955. It also appears that the appeal being No. 13274 of 2015 was disposed of in presence of the respondent No. 4 who claimed that there is no existence of Lamashempur Atimer Jame Mosque. But it appears from the findings of the Appeal Officer passed in appeal No. 13274 of 2015 that the Motwalli of respondent No. 4 namely Musabbir was present in a meeting held by the petitioner Lamashempur Atimer Jame Mosque on 14-6-2016 and put his signature on the resolution sheet in serial No. 1. In that meeting it was decided that for the development of Lamashempur Atimer Jame Mosque, a portion of land to be sold out. Accordingly a sale deed was prepared whereon the Motwalli of respondent No. 4 Musabbir put his signature and thus the respondent No. 4 admitted the existence of the petitioner Lamashempur A timer Jame Mosque. Moreover, it appears from the findings of the Appeal Officer that there are four separate undisputed DP khatian Nos. 260, 146, 327 and 506 were prepared in the name of the petitioner Lamashempur Atimer Jame Mosque which support the existence of the Lamashempur Jame Mosque. Thereafter, the Appeal Officer decided that there is existence of Lamashempur Jame Mosque. His finding is well reasoned, we find nothing to disbelieve the same.
9. It was proved in the appeal that the petitioner has been possessing the land as a mosque and graveyard connecting electric line and paying electricity bill. Annexure-'C' is the photocopy of electricity bill which supports the claim of the petitioner as to connection of electric line and payment of electric bill in the name of petitioner Lamashempur Atimer Jame Mosque.
10. As per contentions of the petitioner, a portion of land is being used for the purpose of graveyard and another portion is used for the mosque which reveals the manner how the petitioner has been possessing the disputed land as mosque and graveyard.
11. On the other hand, the respondent No. 4 failed to prove his claim over the disputed land. It appears from the petition filed by the respondent No. 4 under rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 that he did not state in that petition how the respondent No. 4 became owner and possessor of the disputed land. Even he did not state a single word or sentence as to manner of possession of the disputed land. In that petition it has not been claimed that the landin dispute is being possessed by the respondent No. 4.
12. It appears from the application filed under rule 42A that the respondent No. 4 did not challenge the findings of the Appeal Officer as to existence of the Lamashempur Atimer Jame Mosque and his signature put on the resolution sheet and sale deed as stated in the findings passed in the appeal under rule 31. The application filed under rule 42A contains no specific allegation of fraud. Respondent No. 4 stated in the application under rule 42A that the Appeal Officer admitted the appeal on 25-11-2015 illegally after 6 years and 5 months from the disposal of the Objection Case No. 399 on 27-4-2009 and he illegally condoned 6 years 5 months delay and, as such, committed fraud. But, on perusal of the record it appears that the DP khatian was prepared neither in the name of the petitioner nor in the name of the respondent No. 4. The respondent No. 4 filed Objection Case No. 399 and obtained order in his favour. Admittedly in that objection case the petitioner Lamashempur Atimer Jame Mosque was not party. Subsequently, the petitioner came to know about the objection case and filed an appeal under rule 31 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955. It also appears that considering the facts and circumstances the Appeal Officer condoned the period of Limitation. We are of the view that the Appeal Officer is fully authorized by law to condone delay in filing the appeal if the facts and circumstances permit him. On perusal of the materials on record it reveals that the Appeal Officer rightly condoned the delay considering the existing facts and circumstances of the case. So, condonation of delay in filing of the appeal cannot be considered as fraud. It is settled principle of law that a mere allegation of fraud is not sufficient unless the ingredients of fraud are disclosed in the petition for taking cognizance of allegation. Hence, we are of the view that ingredients of fraud was not detected or disclosed in the petition filed by the respondent No. 4 under rule 42A or proceedings under rules 28-31 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955.
13. The decisions referred by the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent No. 4 are not applicable in the instant case, inasmuch as the facts of both the cases referred by the learned Advocate for the respondent No. 4 are different from the facts of the instant case.
14. We have gone through the facts and-decisions of both the cases. It appears from the case of Mainuddin Ahmed vs Government of People's Republic of Bangladesh and others reported in 7 SCOB (2016) 134 that two Settlement Appeals being Nos. 8970 of 2003 and 11915 of 2008 were filed under rule 31 of the Tenancy Rules, 1955. Settlement Appeal No. 8970 of 2003 was dismissed on contest, but settlement Appeal No. 11915 of 2008 was dismissed in absence of the appellant. The High Court Division stated in the judgment that the Appeal Officer committed a serious error in disposing the settlement appeal No. 11915 of 2008 in absence of the appellant and on 20-8-2009 respondent No. 12 submitted an application to the respondent No. 3 with a complaint of fraudulent entry in the DP khatian as to case property upon stating the fact of his absence at the time of disposal of the said settlement appeal No. 11915 of 2008. On the basis of that allegation respondent No. 3 directed respondent No 5 to submit a report upon carrying out a preliminary investigation under rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955. Having been, thus asked by a superior authority respondent No. 5 conducted an inquiry into the allegation of committing fraud and submitted an elaborate report to respondent No. 3. Through the said investigation, it was revealed that the opponent of the settlement appeal No. 8970 of 2003 and the settlement appeal No. 11915 of 2009 (Mainuddin Ahmed) do not have any physical possession in the property and, thus, the said investigation hinted at the existence of prima-facie elements of fraud. Thereafter the respondent No. 3 settlement officer issued notice under rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955. So, it appears that after detection of existence of prima facie elements of fraud in the aforesaid case, the Settlement Officer has issued notice under rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955.
15. In the case of Rawson Ara Khatun and others vs Md Wais Hossain and others reported in 26 BLC (AD) 12, we find that before issuance of notice under rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 preliminary inquiry was held and having found, prima facie elements of fraud, notice was issued under rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955.
16. But in the instant case no preliminary inquiry was held, no prima facie elements of fraud was detected before issuance of the notice, the application filed under rule 42A contains no specific allegation of fraud, the settlement appeal No. 13274 of 2015 under rule 31 was disposed of on contest in presence of the respondent No. 4, the order passed by the Appeal Officer in appeal No. 13274 of 2015 is legal and well reasoned. Under such circumstances we are of the view the facts of the cases referred by the learned. Advocate for the respondent No. 4 are quite different from the facts of the instant case. So, the decisions referred by the learned Advocate for the respondent No. 4 are not applicable in the instant case.
17. On the other hand, it is pertinent to mention here that the case referred by the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner is very much relevant for the instant case. He referred the case of Zahirul Islam and others vs Government of Bangladesh and others, reported in 65 DLR 168.
18. In that case it has been decided that once appeal has been disposed of on contest under rule 31 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Rules, 1955 no review (.....) lies and the settlement authorities have got no jurisdiction to reopen the matter other than to send the draft publication khatian for final publication under rule 32 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Rules, 1955.
19. We are of the view that if the appeal is disposed of on merit and on contest and the order of the Appeal Officer is well reasoned and there is no doubt as to fraud in the order passed in appeal and the application under rule 42A contains no specific allegation of fraud and the fraud is not, prima facie, detected before issuance of notice, then the Revenue Officer designated as Settlement Officer is not legally empowered to issue a notice under rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955. He can issue notice under rule 42A only after having got, prima facie, elements of fraud otherwise not.
<u>20. The authority/jurisdiction provided to the Revenue Officer with the additional designation of Settlement Officer under rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 is extra-ordinary and special in nature which should not be exercised in general or normal cases rather it should be exercised in extra-ordinary and special cases where there is, prima fade, elements of fraudulent entry in the record-of-rights before final publication. To that effect; to prevent harassment and colourable exercise of authority under rule 42A, the Revenue Officer or Settlement Officer, shall issue notice under rule 42A after being mentally formed decision and satisfied that there is prima facie, element of fraudulent entry in the record-of-rights to save the actual land owners from harassment by the ill motivated litigants in the name of false and fraudulent entry in the record-of-rights.</u>
21. In the light of the above deliberation, we find merit in the Rule.
22. In the result, the Rule is made absolute and it is hereby declared that the Notice bearing Memo No. 31-3-0000.031.33.668.13-48/2(1) dated 17-2-2016 to have been issued by the respondent No. 3, Zonal Settlement Officer, Sylhet, in Miscellaneous Case No. 846 of 2016 filed under rule 42A of the Tenancy Rules, 1955 without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.
Communicate the copy of the judgment and order at once.
Let the judgment and order be served upon the respondents for information and necessary step:
1. The Secretary, Ministry of Land, Bangladesh Secretariat Building, Ramna, Dhaka-1000 (who shall serve it upon all the Deputy Commissioners and Zonal Settlement Officers except Sylhet).
2. The Deputy Commissioner, Sylhet.
3. Zonal Settlement Officer, Zonal Settlement Office, Sylhet.
However, there is no order as to cost.
End.

Mojida alias Majeda Begum and others -------- Defendants-Petitioners
VS
Safia and others ------- Plaintiff-Respondents
full_judgment:
JBM Hassan, J: Similar questions of laws and facts are involved in the above-mentioned writ petitions. Hence, the Rules Nisi issued in those writ petitions have been heard together and are being disposed of by this common judgment.
2. All the writ petitions have been filed challenging the judgment and decree of the Land Survey Tribunal of different districts passed in the respective land survey suits. Although section 145B of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act ("SAT Act") incorporates provisions for challenging judgment and decree of the Land Survey Tribunal by preferring appeal before the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal but at the relevant time of passing those decrees, there was no appellate forum due to which the petitioners of the respective writ petitions being aggrieved by the impugned judgment and decree, filed these writ petitions and obtained the Rules Nisi.
3. Now learned Advocates for the petitioners of respective writ petitions and Mr AM Aminuddin, learned Attorney-General jointly submit that in the meantime the appellate forum has been established and so, by disposing these Rules Nisi, the writ petitioners may be allowed to prefer appeal in their respective jurisdictions challenging the impugned judgment and decree.
4. However, learned Advocates for the petitioners of all writ petitions jointly submit that in the meantime the statutory period for preferring the appeal has already been expired. Despite having no laches/fault on the part of the petitioners, they could not prefer appeal due to non existence of appellate forum and that having no alternative remedy at the relevant time, they filed these writ petitions.
5. We have considered the submissions of learned Advocates and the learned Attorney-General. We have also gone through the relevant provisions of law and other materials on record.
6. Section 145B of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (hereinafter referred to as "the SAT Act") incorporates the provisions regarding appeal against the judgment and decree or order of the Land Survey Tribunal. The same are as follows:
"145B. Land Survey Appellate Tribunal—(1) The Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, establish as many Land Survey Appellate Tribunals as may be required to hear the appeals arising out of the judgment, decree or order of the Land Survey Tribunals.
(2) The Government may, by notification in the official Gazette, fix and alter the territorial limits of the jurisdiction of any Land Survey Appellate Tribunal.
[(3) The Government shall appoint the judge of the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal from among the persons who are District judges.]
[(3A) Until such judge is appointed under sub-section (3), the Government may empower the District Judge as the judge of the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal of the district.
(3B) The District Judge, empowered under sub-section (3A), shall be deemed to be the judge of the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal appointed under sub-section (3). (3C) The Government may, if necessary, appoint one or more Additional District Judges as a judge of the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal to hear appeals transferred by the judge of the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal appointed or empowered under this section.]
(4) No appeal other than the appeals arising out of the judgment, decree or order of the Land Survey Tribunal shall lie in the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal.
(5) Subject to the provision of sub-section
(6), any person aggrieved by any judgment, decree or order of the Land Survey Tribunal may, within three months from the date of such judgment, decree or order, prefer an appeal to the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal. (6) An appeal may be admitted within next three months even after the expiry of the period specified in sub-section (5), if the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal is satisfied with the reasons for delay shown by the appellant"
7. Upon perusal of the aforesaid provisions, it appears that sub-section (5) provides three months time to prefer appeal to the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal from the date of such impugned judgment and decree or order to be passed by the Land Survey Tribunal. Sub-section (6) provides further three months time, if the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal is satisfied with the reasons for delay shown by the appellant.
8. Admittedly, in the meantime 6(six) months time from the date of decree or order have already been expired long before but facts remain that there was no appellate forum so long.
9. The SAT Act is a special law and the limitation period incorporated in the Special Statute cannot be condoned under section 5 of the Limitation Act. Therefore, in the circumstances, a question arises, as to how the aggrieved person, in particular, the writ petitioners will challenge the impugned judgment and decree before the recently established appellate forum.
10. In these context, Mr Md Imam Hassan, learned Advocate for the petitioners of writ petitions No. 5135 of 2018 and 12559 of 2022 has drawn our attention to the case of Bangladesh, represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Education, Dhaka and others vs GMM Mizanur Rahman Bhuiyan and others reported in 2018 (26) BLT (AD) 37, the case of Rama Aba Singale and others vs Sumitrabai and another reported in AIR 1979 Bombay 14 and the case of Dharamsi Morarji Chemical, Co. Ltd. vs Occhavlal Hargovandas Shah reported in AIR 1927 Bombay 480. He also refers to an unreported order dated 15-10-2023 of the Appellate Division passed in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1548 of 2023.
11. From the facts, it appears that although at the time of enactment of section 145B of the SAT Act in 2004, the Statute incorporated the provisions for preferring appeal within 3 months from the date of decree or order but the forum of appeal for the first time established by the State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Act, 2023 Gazetted on 7-6-2023 and by the Gazette Notification dated 23-8-2023, the jurisdiction of Land Survey Appellate Tribunal has been determined under different districts. In the circumstances, since the appellate forum has been established on 23-8-2023, we are of the view that the petitioners can take their grievances to the respective Land Survey Appellate Tribunals by preferring appeal challenging the impugned judgment and decree or order.
12. But section 145B being a special law and in the mean time the statutory limitation period having been expired, the question of condonation of delay has been arisen. The facts as appeared before us are that although the Statute provides definite period of limitation but there was no appellate forum before the aggrieved person to prefer appeal challenging the impugned judgment and decree or order. To appreciate this situation we have noticed a relevant finding incorporated in the decision reported in AIR 1927 Bombay 480 (supra) wherein the High Court Division held as under:
"It seems to me clear that the principle is this that when a party has to do something before a certain day and if upon that day or before that day he cannot do that thing by reason of the act of the Court then he is entitled to an extension of time over that period during which he is delayed by the Court's action. Thus in considering whether or not section 4 applies to this suit, it is necessary in my judgment to consider whether the plaintiffs could have filed their suit during the annual summer vacation."
13. Although, the aforesaid pronouncement was in respect of interpreting section 4 of the Limitation Act and section 10 of the General Clauses Act, but the principle as laid down is, relating to remedy given to an aggrieved party by condoning delay when there was no fault on his part in pursuing the litigation/appeal.
14. In our jurisdiction, the apex Court also enunciated a principle in filing case before the Administrative Tribunal condoning the delay under the Administrative Tribunals Act, a special law for the Government employees who on misconception, filed the writ petition taking their grievances. In disposing of those writ petitions, the Appellate Division finally in the case reported in 2018 (26) BLT (AD) 37 (supra) held as under:
"Since the writ petitioners can seek reliefs before the Administrative Tribunal, we make it clear that if the writ petitioners desire to redress their grievances before the Administrative Tribunal since they had been prosecuting their grievance in the Supreme Court of Bangladesh for a long time, the Administrative Tribunal shall entertain their petitions, if any are filed on condoning the delay under section 14 of the Limitation Act. We also waive the statutory bar applicable to an applicant for filing a departmental appeal before the appellate authority, since they have already moved the High Court Division, the said period of limitation has already expired."
15. Limitation question in preferring appeal before the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal, has not yet been raised before the Appellate Division. However, at the time of disposing of two writ petitions arising out of decree of Land Survey Tribunal, the High Court Division passed an interim order of statusquo and it was adjudicated before the Appellate Division. Their lordships in passing the order on 15-10-2023 in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal Nos. 1548 of 2023 and 1398 of 2023 held as under:
"We have heard the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioner in both the cases and perused the impugned judgment and orders of the High Court Division as well as other materials on record. Upon perusal it appears that section 145B of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 stipulates 3 (three) months' time for preferring appeal before the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal.
Thus we are inclined to modify the order of the High Court Division in the following manner:
"Meanwhile status quo in respect of possession of the suit land shall continue till 3 (three) months from the date of establishment of the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal or from the date of empowering the District Judge as the Judge of the concerned Land Survey Appellate Tribunal under. section 145B(3A) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 (as amended in 2023)"
With the above observations and modification of the order, these Civil Petitions for Leave to Appeal are disposed of."
16. From the above order, it is apparent that due to non existence of the Land Survey Appellate Tribunal, the Apex Court extended the force of order of statusquo till 3 (three) months from the date of establishment of the said Appellate Tribunal. But here in these matters, 3 months limitation period have already been passed from the date of establishment of appellate forum. Yet on identical circumstances, we consider that due to non existence of Land Survey Appellate Tribunal, the writ petitioners could not challenge the impugned judgment and decree or order and this situation led them to file writ petitions obtaining Rules Nisi in their respective writ petitions. Thus, they have remained under the litigations before this Court so long.
17. Now, since the appellate forum has been established, the petitioners are at liberty to prefer the appeal.
18. In this context, learned Attorney-General also submits that in view of the above-mentioned ratios of our jurisdiction as well as India, the Appellate Tribunal can consider their respective appeals, if filed, along with an application for condonation of delay in accordance with section 14 of the Limitation Act.
19. Although there is no scope to condone the delay occurred under the special law, even then section 29 of the Limitation Act incorporates provisions of savings clause which run as follows:
"29. Savings:—(1) Nothing in this Act shall affect section 25 of the Contract Act, 1872.
(2) Where any special law prescribes for any suit, appeal or application a period of limitation different from the period prescribed therefor by the first schedule, the provision of section 3 shall apply, as if such period were prescribed therefor in that schedule, and for the purpose of determining any period of limitation prescribed for any suit, appeal or application by any special law—(a) the provisions contained in section 4, sections 9 to 18, and section 22 shall apply only in so far as, and to the extent to which, they are not expressly excluded by such special laws and (b) the remaining provisions of this Act shall not apply.
(3) ....................
(4) ......................
20. On perusal of the aforesaid provisions, it is clear that the provisions contained in section 4, sections 9 to 18, and section 22 shall apply only in so far as, and to the extent to which, they are not expressly excluded by the special law.
<u>21. Here the applicability of section 9 to 18 i.e. inclusive of section 14 have not been excluded expressly by the SAT Act and since, the writ petitions are being filed under the constitutional jurisdiction of this Court, certainly section 14 shall be applicable to condone the delay in appeals to be filed by those writ petitioners.</u>
<u>22. Considering all these aspects and regard being had to the above, we are not inclined to dispose of the writ petitions on merit. Rather, we are of the view that the writ petitions shall be disposed of giving a liberty to the petitioners to prefer appeal before their respective appellate jurisdiction to testify the impugned judgment and decree or order of the Land Survey Tribunal.</u>
23. In the light of the above observations, all the Rules Nisi are disposed of with the following directions:
(i) The petitioners are at liberty to prefer appeal before the respective Land Survey Appellate Tribunals with an application for condonation of delay and, if so filed, the respective Appellate Tribunal shall consider the application as well as the appeal in accordance with section 14 read with section 29 of the Limitation Act. (ii) Send down the lower Court's records in respect of writ petitions where the same have arrived in the meantime.
(iii) The petitioners and the respondents are at liberty to take back all the original certified copies annexed with the respective writ petitions or affidavit-in-opposition or application(s) or affidavit(s) on furnishing photocopies thereof duly attested by the respective learned Advocates.
(iv) The interim order of stay/status quo passed by this Court, if any, be extended for further 4(four) months from date or until filing the appeal, whichever is earlier.
End.

lawyer:
Murad Reza, Senior Advocate with Mejbahur Rahman, Advocates—For the Petitioner. 
Morshad Ahmed Khan with Shafiqul Kabir Khan and Mirza Sultan-Alraza, Advocates—For the Respondent Nos. 1-3.
parties:
Oriental Oil Company Limited --------- Petitioner
VS
RFL Plastic Limited and others ---------- Respondents
full_judgment:
The petitioner, which is a company incorporated in Bangladesh (hereinafter referred to either as the petitioner or the petitioner-company) under the Companies Act, 1994 (briefly, the Companies Act) is seeking winding up of RFL Plastic Limited, which is also an incorporated company in Bangladesh under the Companies Act, having its registered office at Barabo, Tarabo Paurashava, Rupganj, 1460, Narayanganj (hereinafter referred to either as RFL Plastic or the debtor-company or the respondent-company), by invoking section 241 of the Companies Act on the ground, inter alia, that RFL Plastic is unable to pay its debt.
2. The averments made by the petitioner-company in its petition under section 241 of the Companies Act, briefly, are that it entered into an agreement with RFL Plastic (the respondent-company) on 12-12-2016 for supplying lubricant from 12-12-2016 to 11-12-2018. After receiving the work order, the petitioner-company supplied lubricant on a regular basis and payments were also made regularly by the respondent-company. At times, the respondent-company made less payment than the invoiced amount. Lastly the respondent-company issued work orders between March to May 2018 and the petitioner-company supplied the lubricant accordingly without raising any issue as to quality or quantity. The petitioner-company sent invoices against supply of lubricants based on the work orders. The respondent-company failed to pay against those invoices. Total outstanding amount against those invoices and short payment against earlier invoices came to a total Taka 1,38,17,735.34, breakdown of the said outstanding amount was provided to the respondent-company in a table. Several e-Mails and letters were sent to the respondent-company requesting to make the payments but no payments were made. Finding no other options, the petitioner-company sent a Legal Notice on 10-1-2019 and, after expiry of more than 21 (twenty one) days of receipt of the aforesaid Legal Notice, when the petitioner-company was not paid off its dues, it approached this Court. And, this Court having heard the matter, simply issued a Show Cause Notice on 16-6-2019, instead of admitting the instant petition.
3. The statements made by the RFL Plastic (the respondent-company) in its affidavit-in-opposition, in short, are that Mr Ahsan Khan Chowdhury (respondent No. 2) is a prominent businessman of Bangladesh who is the key person (i.e. the Chairman and CEO) of PRAN-RFL Group, and the respondent-company is one of the sister concerns of PRAN-RFL Group. The petitioner-company is a sister concern of Alliance Group (hereinafter referred to as the Alliance Group) of which Mr Syed Ali Jowher Rizvi is the Group Chairman (hereinafter referred to as Alliance Group Chairman). He is also the promoter and one of the major shareholders and Directors of the petitioner-company. M/s Global FMCG Distribution Company (shortly, Global FMCG) is a registered partnership firm actually/ beneficially owned by the Alliance Group Chairman and his son, Mr Syed Yasser Haider Rizvi. Both of them (Mr jowher Rizvi and Mr Haider Rizvi) are the signatories of all the Bank accounts maintained by the said partnership firm, but the said firm is officially formed in the names of two employees of Alliance Group. The back-ground history of establishing the Global FMCG, as stated by the respondent-company, is that around late 2014, Alliance Group Chairman approached the respondent No. 2 who agreed to purchase Cola in PET bottles on short-term credit basis by Alliance Group from PRAN-RFL Group for the drink produced by Alliance Group with the brand name 'Virgin'. Alliance Group Chairman informed that because of some of his impediments he was considering doing the said business transaction through a partnership firm to be registered in the names of his employees, keeping the financial affairs of the said firm under his control and, accordingly, Global FMCG was formed vide Deed of Agreement for Partnership dated 9-12-2014 and was registered with the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies and Firms (RISC) on 20-12-2014, and thereafter the agreement dated 15-1-2015 (hereinafter referred to as the 'Cola Supply Agreement') was signed by and between a company of the respondent No. 2, namely, Mymensingh Agro Ltd and the said Global FMCG. Although the initial validity of the Cola Supply Agreement was for 3 (three) years, the PRAN-RFL Group supplied the Cola for about two years, because the Alliance Group failed to maintain regular payment of price of the delivered Cola in compliance with the Cola Supply Agreement. As a result, an amount of Taka 2,10,41,113 remained unpaid, for which around the last quarter of 2016 the respondent No. 2 had series of meetings with the Alliance Group Chairman to resolve the said issue of non-payment and, eventually, it was agreed that PRAN-RFL Group would purchase lubricants from Alliance Group for an initial period of about two years and out of the price of the lubricants, the unpaid price for the Cola would be adjusted/ set-off by PRAN-RFL Group. Accordingly, Deed of Agreement dated 12-12-2016 was signed by and between the RFL Plastic and the petitioner-company (hereinafter referred to as the 'Lubricant Supply Agreement').
4. The petitioner-company then started supplying the lubricants and the PRAN-RFL Group started to adjust the unpaid sale price for the Cola from the price of the lubricants; but the Alliance Group requested to make the adjustment from subsequent invoices. It so happened that whenever the PRAN-RFL Group attempted to set-off the unpaid sale price for Cola from the price of the lubricants, the Alliance Group on various excuses requested to adjust from subsequent invoices. In such a situation, the respondent No. 2 once again had meetings and negotiations with the Alliance Group Chairman in December 2017 and April 2018 and ultimately in April-May 2018 PRAN-RFL Group adjusted an aggregate amount of Taka 1,36,42,607 only out of the price of the lubricants and, as such, an amount of Taka 73,98,506 only remained unadjusted. Thereafter, when the Alliance Group stopped supplying any lubricants to the PRAN-RFL Group, once again the respondent No. 2 and the Alliance Group Chairman had meetings to resolve the issue, but to no effect and ultimately the petitioner through their lawyer issued Legal Notice dated 10-1-2019, which was replied to by the respondent-company on 29-1-2019. Even after filing of the Company Matter, the respondent No. 2 had meeting with the Alliance Group Chairman in October 2020 for an amicable solution, but the said effort was unsuccessful. In the above circumstances, on 6- 1-2021 these respondents along with the said sister concern, namely, Mymensingh Agro Ltd, as plaintiffs, filed Money Suit No. 4 of 2021 against Mr Syed Ali Jowher Rizvi, the petitioner-company, Mr Syed Yasser Haider Rizvi, Global FMCG and its alleged partners for recovery of Taka 73,98,506 only being the balance sale price of Cola after setting-off an amount of Taka 1,36,42,607 only out of the price of the lubricants.
5. Mr Mejbahur Rahman, the learned Advocate for the petitioner-company, contends that the amount owed to the petitioner-company is not disputed in that RFL Plastic never denied or disputed either about the quality and quantity or as to the outstanding amount; even RFL Plastic in their reply to statutory Legal Notice did not raise any dispute with regard to the outstanding amount. By referring to Form-1, annexed by the respondents, he contends that the petitioner-company is a partnership concern between Mohammad Abdul Hai and Manjur Kadin He contends that Global FMCG is not a sister concern of the petitioner-company and the current Directors of the petitioner-company are also not a party to the partnership firm, but two of the Directors of the petitioner-company have been made joint signatories of the accounts as per the partnership agreement of the said partnership firm. He next submits that despite the debt being acknowledged by the RFL Plastic, the same is not being paid off by RFL Plastic and, therefore, by the deeming provisions of section 242 of the Companies Act, the Company Court should hold that RFL Plastic is in fact unable to pay the debt. 7. Against the submissions advanced by the learned Advocate for the petitioner-company, the learned Advocate for the respondent-company, Mr Morshed Ahmed Khan, contends that since the respondent-company submitted affidavit-in-opposition on 16-9-2020 against this Court's Show Cause and a supplementary thereto on 3-11-2020 having stated therein that the partnership firm, namely, Global FMCG Distribution Ltd is a sister concern of the petitioner-company and this partnership firm owes Taka 2,10,41,113 to the respondent-company but the respondent-company is not paying the money owed to the petitioner-company, there is no point in filing the instant application for winding up of the respondent-company without first resolving the claim of the respondent-company. Mr Morshed Ahmed Khan next submits that in the backdrop of existence of the aforesaid contract for adjustment/set off, which was entered into by Mr Syed Ali Jowher Rizvi being the Group Chairman of the petitioner-company under its implied authority as required by section 126 of the Companies Act, the contract for adjustment/set off is binding upon the petitioner-company.
