9. He then submits that the legal position as established by our Apex Court is that in order to make out a case for winding up, the petitioner has to show that firstly, the respondent-company is commercially insolvent as the company admits the debts but is unable to pay the same or there are more than one creditor and the company, though willing to pay the debt of one creditor, but is unable to pay all the creditors' entire debts and, secondly, it has lost its substratum. He argues that in this particular case, the petitioner has not come up with such facts, rather the case of the petitioner is that the respondent-company is unable to pay its debts owed to the petitioner company only. He submits that for this Court, it will be a futile exercise to admit this application and, therefore, this petition is liable to be summarily rejected. By putting forward the above submissions, the learned Advocate for the respondents prays for rejecting this application for winding up with exemplary costs. In support of his above submissions, he refers to the cases of (1) Bangladesh Tyres Ltd vs Agrani Bank and others, 43 DLR (AD) 164, (2) Amenehispahani vs Free School Street Property Ltd, 3 BLC (AD) 212, (3) Amin Scales Limited vs Md Yakub, 1987 BLD (AD) 259 = 39 DLR (AD) 201, (4) Mohidul Islam vs Century Properties Development Ltd, 7 BLC 248, (5) Ambala Cold Storage (Pvt) Ltd vs Prime Insurance Co. Ltd, reported in 56 DLR 422 and (6) Amin (Md) vs Bengal Shipping Lines Ltd 60 DLR 444.
10. Upon perusal of the application for the winding up of the respondent-company, affidavits-in-opposition and on reading the relevant statutory laws as well as the case laws, and having considered the submissions of the learned Advocates for both the sides, it appears to this Court that the following issues are to be adjudicated upon by this Court: (1) whether the expression 'unable to pay the debts', as occurring in sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, is applicable when the debtor-company is not unable as such but is 'unwilling to pay the debts', (2) whether the expression 'unable to pay the debts' implies that the debtor-company is 'commercially insolvent' or has lost its substratum, (3) whether in a winding up application the debts in question are required to be an admitted debt for allowing an application for winding up, (4) what is meant by the expression 'bona fide dispute' and if there is a bonafide dispute against a debt, whether the question of 'neglect to pay', the condition for deeming 'unable to pay the debts', arises at all, (5) in this case, whether the respondent-company is unable to pay the debts owed to the petitioner-company or it is unwilling to pay because of its counter claim against the petitioner-company and (6) whether, pursuant to issuance of Show Cause Notice by this Court upon the respondents, it is obligatory for this Court to admit the instant application towards its final disposal.
11. Part V, which consists of sections 234 to 321 of the Companies Act, deals with the various issues of winding up of a company, such as modes of winding up (i.e. winding up by Court, voluntary winding up by members/creditors or voluntary winding up under the supervision of the Court), contributories' responsibilities, powers of Court, official liquidator, enforcement of and appeals from orders etc. Since the present case is concerned with winding up of the respondent-company by Court, for an effective and inclusive adjudication of the issue Nos. 1 to 4, as framed by this Court hereinbefore, it would be useful if the provisions of sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act are quoted. Section 241 of the Companies Act runs as follows:
241. Circumstances in which company may be wound up by Court.— A company may be wound up by the Court;—
(i) if the company has by special resolution resolved that the company be wound up by the Court; or
(ii) if default is made in filing the statutory report or in holding the statutory meeting; or;
(iii) if the company does not commence its business within a year from its incorporation, or suspends its business for a whole year; or
(iv) if the number of members is reduced, in the case of a private company below two, or, in the case of any other company, below seven; or
(v) if the company is unable to pay its debts: or
(vi) if the Court is of opinion that it is just and equitable that the company should be wound up.
<u>12. The provisions of section 241 of the Companies Act provide for as many as 6 (six) circumstances in which a company may be wound up by the Court. Given that section 241 of the Companies Act empowers the Company Court by employing the word 'may', it is discretion for the Court to decide as to whether it should pass an Order for winding up of a company. It means that while the Court may order for winding up of a company upon finding any of the circumstances stated in section 241 of the Companies Act, it may also decline to order winding up of a company, of course, by exercising its discretionary power judiciously, even if one or more circumstances under section 241 of the Companies Act are found to be present by the Court.</u>
13. In this case, the circumstance numbered as (v) under section 241 of the Companies Act is relevant. So, this Court requires to examine the circumstances which might be regarded as 'inability to pay debts' of a company. Section 242 of the Companies Act seeks to define and determine when a company's circumstances shall be deemed as 'unable to pay its debts'. Let me, therefore, look at the provisions of section 242 of the Companies Act, which run as follows:
242. Company when deemed unable to pay its debts.—(1) A company shall be deemed to be unable to pay its debts—(i) if a creditor, by assignment or otherwise, to whom the company is indebted for a sum exceeding five hundred take then due, has served on the company, by causing the same to be delivered by registered post or other-wise at its registered office, a demand under his hands requiring the company to pay the sum so due and the company has for three weeks thereafter neglected to pay the sum or to secure or compound for it to the reasonable satisfaction of the creditor; or (ii) if execution or other process issued on a decree or order of any court in favour of a creditor of the company is returned unsatisfied in whole or in part; or (iii) if it is proved to the satisfaction of the Court that the company is unable to pay its debts, the Court shall take into account the contingent and prospective liabilities of the company.
(2) .................
<u>14. The provisions of section 242 of the Companies Act lay down the conditions of deeming a company's inability to pay its debts. The legal requirements for deeming inability of a company to pay its debts are; firstly, the amount payable must be certain, being more than of Taka 500 (Taka five hundreds); secondly, the company has received a notice from the creditor demanding the sum so due; thirdly, the company did not pay off or compound with the creditor within three weeks of the receipt of the demand notice and, fourthly, despite the company being issued with an execution process pursuant to a Decree or Order of any Court, it fails to satisfy the said execution process wholly or in part. However, the said criteria do not specify the exact situations or the events for passing a winding up order by the Court.</u>
15. Now, if the provisions of sections 241(v) and 242 of the Companies Act are read together, the one obvious meaning derives therefrom is that a company may be wound up ^ by the Company Court if it is satisfactorily proved before the Court that the company is unable to pay its debts, or "deemed" to have been unable to pay its debts. What is debt, is no more a res Integra. In course of interpreting section 25 of the Contract Act, 1872 and section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, the Courts of this sub-continent in a catena of cases have defined the expression 'debt' as a liability to pay off an ascertainable sum of money to the creditor in the present or in future. But if the company disputes the creditor's debts/ demand i.e. if the company either makes a counter-claim or totally denies the creditor's claim upon substantiating the said dispute with evidence, what should be the role of the Company Court? Nothing has been prescribed in sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act to overcome the said dilemma.
16. In order to have the answer to the question posed, which will ultimately adjudicate upon the issue Nos. 1-4, as framed by this Court hereinbefore, this Court requires to make a survey on the case laws of home and abroad, so that the definitions and meanings of the expressions 'bona fide dispute', 'undisputedly ascertained', 'admitted debts' 'unable to pay the debts', 'unwilling to pay', 'deemed to have been unable to pay the debts' 'neglect to pay', 'commercially insolvent' and 'losing a company's substratum', which have been stated in the pleadings and employed in the submissions made by the learned Advocates for the contending parties, can be gathered.
17. In the case of Amin Scales Limited & another vs Md Yakiib 1987 BLD (AD) 259 = 39 DLR (AD) 201, the appellant Amin Scales Ltd by way of preferring appeals before the Hon'ble Appellate Division challenged the legality of the Order of admission of the winding up application as well as the Order refusing to stay operation of the proceedings passed by the Company Court in Company Matter No. 27 of 1996. While dismissing the appeals, the Hon'ble Appellate Division laid down the following principle:
A mere filing of an application containing some allegations that the company failed to pay its debts is not sufficient for its admission. R ather, great care should be taken in admitting an application for winding up as it is likely to create alarm in the minds of all creditors of the company, divert its customers away and to paralyze its business. A winding up order will not be made on a debt which is bona fide disputed by the company. If there is genuine dispute, petition may be dismissed or stayed and an injunction may be granted restraining the advertisement of the petition.
18. In the case of Ameneh Ispahani vs Free School Street Property Ltd and another 3 BLC (AD) 212, the petitioner Ameneh Ispahani claiming herself to be a creditor of the respondent-company made an application before the Company Court for a winding up order against it on the ground of its neglect and inability to pay her outstanding debts. The Company Court dismissed it on the ground of bona fide dispute. When the petitioner sought leave to appeal, the Hon'ble Appellate Division dismissed it on the same ground.
19. In the case of Ambala Cold Storage (Pot) Ltd vs Prime Insurance Co. Ltd 56 DLR 422, the petitioner prayed for winding up of the respondent-company on the ground that the respondent-company has miserably failed to pay its liabilities, which were claimed by the petitioner-company under various insurance policies. In the affidavit-in-opposition the respondent-company denied the material allegations and further stated that the petition had been filed as a pressure tactic to recover the so-called dues which are highly disputed by the respondent-company. While dismissing the application for winding up, the Company Court observed as follows—
The claim is not undisputedly ascertained, and unless it is admitted it cannot be said it is a debt and the respondent company is liable to pay the debt. Winding up of a company by Court for debt is not called for where there is a bona fide dispute relating to the existence of the debt.
20. On the other hand, upon perusal of the contending parties' statements and examining the annexed papers if it appears to the Company Court that the respondent-company is, in fact, 'unable to pay its debts' due to its 'commercial insolvency', in that event, the Company Court should pass an Order of winding up of the company as was held in the case of Agrani Bank vs Bangladesh Tyres Ltd 43 DLR (AD) 164. In the said case, by filing an application for winding up under sections 162 and 163 read with section 166 of the Companies Act, 1913 (which are the corresponding provisions to sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 1994), the petitioner (Agrani Bank) prayed for winding of the respondent-company, namely, the Bangladesh Tyres Ltd on the ground that the respondent-company was neglecting to pay its debts on demand. The respondent-company by filing affidavit-in-opposition denied the allegations brought against it, and came up with a counter claim against the petitioner-Bank. It was the claim of the respondent-company that the debt/claim is a disputed one and the dispute is bona fide. But, the Company Court vide its Judgment dated 27-11-1986 ordered the respondent-company to be wound up. The respondent-company, then, preferred Company Appeal No. 17 of 1986 before a Division Bench of the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh [it is worthwhile to jot down here that at that relevant point of time, there was a misconceived practice in the Supreme Court of Bangladesh that an appeal used to be preferred before the Division Bench, at first, against the Judgment of the Company Court and, thereafter, the aggrieved party could file Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal (CPLA) before the Hon'ble Appellate Division]. The Division Bench of the High Court Division allowed the appeal setting aside the Judgment and Order passed by the Company Bench, against which the creditor-Agrani Bank preferred CPLA. The appeal was allowed and the verdict of the Company Bench was restored upon setting aside the Judgment and Order passed by the Division Bench. And, in doing so, their Lordships of the Hon'ble Appellate Division established the following principle: "The basis of an Order for winding up of a company on the ground of its inability to pay its debts is always insolvency". Then, our Hon'ble Appellate Division also laid down the definition of 'commercial insolvency' at para 22 of the Judgment, which is quoted below:
A Company must be found to be commercially insolvent when its existing and probable assets are insufficient to meet the existing liabilities, it is heavily indebted to various creditors, all its assets being in mortgage or in pledge, and there is no possible chance of a profit being made or its business carried out.
21. In course of laying down the principle, our Hon'ble Appellate Division heavily relied upon the case of the Punjab Flying Club Limited AIR (1933) (Lahore) 301, wherein it was held that what the Court has to see in a case like this is whether the company is 'commercially insolvent', i.e., whether it is unable to meet its current liabilities, although the assets when realised including uncalled capital exceed its liabilities (Halsbury's Laws of England, Vol. V, p. 397), as observed by Lord Wrenbury:
In such a case it is useless to say that if the assets of the company are realised there will be ample to pay 20 shillings in the pound: this is not the test. A company may be at the same time insolvent and wealthy. It may have wealth locked up in investment not presently realizable but although this be so, yet if it has not assets available to meet its current liabilities it is commercially insolvent and may be wound up; (Buckley's Law and Practice under the Companies Acts, page 364).
22. Ever since the ratio was laid down in the aforecited 1933's case of Punjab Flying Club Ltd, the Indian Courts have been following it for decades without questioning its propriety, as are evident from the cases subsequent to the afore-cited decision of 1933. In the case of Vanaspati Industries Ltd vs Prabhu Dayal Hari Ram 11950J 20 Comp Case 311, it was held that the expression commercially insolvent' means that the assets of the company are such and its existing liabilities are such as to make it reasonably certain that the existing and probable assets would be insufficient to meet the existing liabilities. Thereafter, in Sri Shanmugar Mills Ltd vs SK Dharmaraja Nadar [19691 39 Comp Case 297, it was held that where the debts of the company could not be paid without selling its machinery and building and if the machinery and building were to be sold, the mill could not run, the company would necessarily have to be wound up. Then, in Registrar of Companies vs MK Brothers (P.) Ltd. MAN LI/LIP/0137/1976, the company was wound up by the Court as it had found that the company had incurred loss to the tune of Rs. 8,95,147 and the company had virtually no fixed assets. It was further found that the loss and expenditure incurred by the company are far in excess and the share capital of the company had virtually disappeared.
23. Courts of our jurisdiction (both the High Court Division and the Hon'ble Appellate Division) also have been following the said principles since the date of pronouncement of the Judgment by the Hon'ble Appellate Division in the case of Agrani Bank vs Bangladesh Tyres Ltd 43 DLR (AD) 164 (which is already cited and discussed hereinbefore), wherein our Hon'ble Appellate Division when found that there were a number of creditors in addition to the petitioner-Agrani Bank and the aggregate amount of all the creditors exceeded the total value of all the movable and immovable properties and assets of the respondent-company, it held that the respondent-company had become commercially insolvent, for which the respondent-company was 'unable to pay its debts'. In the aforesaid case, the Hon'ble Appellate Division also found the situation No. (vi) under section 241 of the Companies Act, namely, 'if the Court is of opinion that it is just and equitable that the company should be wound up', as it appeared to the Hon'ble Appellate Division that the 'substratum' of the respondent-company had also been lost and, ultimately, it ordered liquidation of the respondent-company on the 'just and equitable' ground.
24. Under what circumstances the respondent-company can be said to have lost its 'substratum'? It is now well settled that the substratum of the company is said to have disappeared when the object for which a company was incorporated no more exists or the object has substantially failed, or when it is impossible for the company to run its the business except at a loss, or the existing and possible assets are insufficient to meet the current and contingent liabilities. 'Losing of substratum of a company' has not been mentioned in section 241 of the Companies Act as one of the situations for winding up of a company. By judicial pronouncements, it has been ruled that 'losing substratum of a company' falls within ambit of the situation No. (vi) under section 241 of the Companies Act (i.e. within the scope of 'just and equitable ground'), which is a wide-ranging ground capable of embracing/attracting various peculiar circumstances for winding up of a company. The situations, such as (1) carrying on the business by causing harm to the decade-old trade mark of another company i.e. against the national policy, as has been held in the case of COSCO Shipping (South East Asia) Pte Ltd vs COSCO (Bangladesh) Shipping Lines Ltd and another 28 ALR (HCD) 1 = 28 BLC 609, (2) conducting a company's business against the interest of the State i.e. when the activities of a company prejudice the greater interest of the public, (3) minority shareholders' loss of confidence in the probity of the Board of Directors, (4) deadlock in the management etc do fall within the scope of situation No. (vi) of section 241 of the Companies Act (i.e. within the periphery of the 'just and equitable' ground).
25. Applying the aforestated principles, latterly, in the case of Mohidul Islam vs Centunj Properties Development Ltd and others, reported in 7 BLC 248, the petitioner purchased an apartment from the respondent-company by entering into a deed of agreement wherein the company committed to complete the said project within 24 months from the date of commencement of work, i.e. February, 1997. When the company failed, the petitioner asked the respondent-company to complete the construction within 25-11-1999 by furnishing an undertaking, to which the respondent-company agreed. The company ultimately failed to complete the project and the petitioner claimed compensation on the basis of Clause 41 of the agreement. The company issued two post-dated cheques, being No. 03A0337880 dated 27-12-2000 for Taka 5,46,000 and No. 03A0337136 dated 15-2-2000 for Taka 2,22,000 but both of them bounced when they were placed for collection. The petitioner, thereafter, wrote to the company on 20-4-2000 to settle the matter amicably within 15 days upon receipt of his letter but the company did not respond. The petitioner caused a statutory notice issued on 8-5-2000 under section 242 of the Companies Act through his lawyer for payment of Taka 9,10,000 being the outstanding amount payable as on 30-4-2000. The respondent-company's lawyer replied denying the claim and asked to refer the matter to arbitration under Clause 40 of the agreement. The petitioner then sought to make out a case before this Court that since the respondent-company has admitted the outstanding dues, the company is liable to be wound up.
26. While rejecting the application under sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, the Company Court observed as follows—
It appears from the papers available on record that the petitioner has hopelessly failed to make out a case for winding up of the company. The claim is only of Taka (nine) lacs and odd as compensation but he has failed to show that the assets of the company are not sufficient to meet his claim and the company's substratum is gone. Petitioner has also failed to show that the respondent-company is commercially insolvent or that it has admitted that it is unable to pay. In fact, the petitioner has admitted that the company is a running company.
27. Reverting to the facts of the case in hand, it is the case of the petitioner that since the outstanding liability to the petitioner-company has never been denied by the respondent company, after expiry of the three weeks of receipt of the demand notice, this Court should pass a winding up Order. It is the further case of the petitioner-company that the respondent-company's attempt of setting off the liabilities of Global FMCG Distribution Company, which is being treated and showed by the respondent-company as a sister concern of the petitioner-company, is bound to fail inasmuch as even if Global FMCG Distribution Company is treated as a sister concern of the petitioner-company, nevertheless, the respondent-company cannot evade their liability under sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, as there is no provision under the Companies Act allowing adjustments of the money owed to the petitioner with a third party.
28. In an endeavour to make out his above-stated case, he relied on the ratio laid down, and observations made, in some cases of foreign jurisdictions and of our own jurisdiction, which are (1) the case of Dena Bank vs Khatau Dyes and Fibres Ltd, 1992(3) Born CR 317, wherein the following observations were made by the Bombay High Court: 'when the debt due by the company to the petitioners is not disputed, it is not enough that the company has the ability to pay the debt; if the company chooses not to pay debt due to the petitioners, the Court will have no choice but to pass an order for winding up the company. By non-payment of the undisputed debt within the period of statutory demand, the company is deemed unable to pay its debts and where the company is unable to pay its debts, winding up ought generally to follow in the public interest, so that the public does not unwarily deal with the company and jeopardises its interests. The petitioners have established that the debt is clear, valid in law, unimpeachable and are entitled to a winding up order ex debito justitiae"; (2) the case of National Bank of Pakistan vs The Punjab National Silk Mills Ltd reported in PLD 1969 (Lahore) 194, wherein the petitioner-Bank filed an application for winding up of the respondent-company on the ground of its failure to pay an ascertained sum of money which the company had not denied and the Court held: 'a winding up petition is a legitimate method of enforcing payment of a just debt. A creditor who is unable to obtain the payment of his debt has the right ex debito justitiae to winding up order'; (3) the case of Cornhill Insurance PLC vs Improvement Services Ltd reported in (1986) BCLC 26 Ch.D, wherein the Chancery Division of the Supreme Court of England and Wales held that where the debt is undisputed and yet the company refuses to pay, a winding up petition is maintainable; (4) the case of BRTC vs Ashraf Jute Mills Ltd, 43 DLR 240, wherein it was held that if the amount of money owed is clear, valid in law, the creditor is entitled to a winding up Order and (5) the case of Raj Kumar and Brother vs Organic Chem Oils Ltd reported in (1998) 93 Company Cases 386, wherein there was evidence on record that a certain amount of money was lawfully due to the petitioner and the respondent-company, despite being put on notice, intentionally failed to pay the same and, in such circumstances, the Court held that 'the company was unable to pay the debt due to the petitioner and, accordingly, it was ordered to be wound up upon holding that—
'the law embodied in section 241 is clear and unambiguous. Section 241(v) of the Act does not impose any pre-condition or qualification for an application to be filed seeking winding up of a company. All that is required is the existence of a claim for an ascertained sum of money, duly acknowledged and owed by the company, which remains unpaid despite a statutory notice being issued upon the company making a demand for payment of the same. Such inability on the part of the company to make payment of the sum that is due and outstanding indicates an inability on the part of the company to pay its debt. In my considered view, the lest in subjective. More often than not, when a notice is issued under section 242(1)(i) of the Act demanding payment of money which is due, the issue of bona fide dispute is usually set up as a defense to refuse the payment. However, when such a dispute does not relate directly to the amount which is admittedly due to the claimant, a defence cannot be set up on that specific ground to deny payment that is due and owing to the claimant. Moreover, mere assertion as to the existence of a dispute between the parties shall not be enough, it must relate to a bona fide dispute. In my view, this is the intendment of the Legislatures, otherwise, the purport and intent of section 241(v) would be rendered ineffective.'
29. Per contra, it is the position of the respondent-company that no money is due from and/or payable by the RFL Plastic (respondent-company) to the petitioner-company, as the claimed amount has been adjusted/set off as per the verbal agreement by and between the Chairman of the RFL Plastic (respondent No. 2) and the petitioner-company's Group Chairman Mr Syed Ali Jowher Rizvi. Further, one of the concerns of the respondent Group, namely, Mymensingh Agro Limited, along with the respondent Nos.1-2 have filed Money Suit No.4 of 2021 against the Chairman of the petitioner-company, Mr Syed Ali Jowher Rizvi, the petitioner-company, Mr Syed Yaseer Haider Rizvi, M/s. Global FMCG Distribution Company and its alleged partners for recovery of Taka 73,98,506 only being the balance sale price of Cola after adjustment/set off of an amount of Taka 1,36,42,607 only out of the price of the lubricants. It is also the position of the respondent-company that the claim of the petitioner-company is heavily and bonafide disputed by the respondents.
30. In a scenario, such as the case in hand, it is incumbent upon the Company Court to initially determine whether the respondent-company is 'unable to pay' or is 'unwilling to pay' its debts. If the Company Court can primarily come to a finding that though the company is capable of paying the creditor's demand, but due to the company's counter-claim or outright denial of the demand, it is not willing to pay, the said demand, then, the next hurdle for the Company Court to encounter and surmount is to see whether the company's said unwillingness is an act actuated by whimsicality and irrationality; that is to say, whether the option of the respondent-company as to abstaining from making payment against the creditor's demand can be regarded as a mala fide inaction or the respondent-company's decision as to non-payment of the creditor's demand can be considered by the Court as a bona fide choice. To deal with these situations, our High Court Division and the Hon'ble Appellate Division as well as the Courts of foreign jurisdictions have laid down the principle, as has been derived from the overview of the cases cited hereinbefore and thereby garnered by this Court, that when the respondent-company's counter claim or denial of the creditor's demand appears to the Company Court to be not a mere attempt to defeat the creditor's demand, rather the Company Court comes to a conclusion that the issue requires a proper adjudication either by the Civil Court or by any other competent forum, the Company Court should consider it as a bona fide dispute.
31. Further, from the literal meanings of the provisions of sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act as well as from the observations made and ratio laid down in the cases examined by this Court hereinbefore, it is the considered view of this Court that if the debt is 'bona fide disputed', there cannot be 'neglect to pay' within section 242(1)(i) of the Companies Act. And, when there is no neglect, the circumstance No. (v) 'the company is unable to pay its debts', as set out in section 241 of the Companies Act, does not arise and, consequently, the deeming provisions under section 242 of the Companies Act do not come into play.
32. Having adjudicated upon the issue Nos. 1-4, now, I may embark upon examination of the issue No. 5, namely, in this case, whether the respondent-company is unable to pay the debts owed to the petitioner-company or it is unwilling to pay because of its counter-claim against the petitioner-company.
33. From the audit report of the PRAN-RFL Group, it transpires that the group is one of the largest conglomerates of Bangladesh as it has an investment of more than 2,000 (two thousand) crores of Taka in its different businesses, which includes the respondent-company. And, from the balance sheet of the respondent-company (namely, RFL Plastic), it is evident that the said company is a solvent company. Thus, this Court finds that the respondent-company is not 'unable to pay its debts', rather it is disputing the petitioner-company's claim by placing before this Court certain apparently plausible transactions between the two Groups of Companies.
34. In the light of the admitted facts that the petitioner-company's 2 (two) Directors are the signatories of the Global FMCG which is evidently registered with the address of the petitioner-company, prima facie this Court finds that the financial transactions of the petitioner-company might have nexus with that of the Global FMCG and, therefore, this Court holds that the dispute is bona fide which requires adjudication by the Civil Court.
<u>35. In this case, thus, it is evident that the respondent-company is not willing to pay. If a debtor is merely unwilling to pay his debts, then the usual course of seeking remedy should be a suit, inasmuch as a suit is the straightforward course for proving one's claim directly and then executing the Decree. And, if his debt is undisputed, the Decree shall follow easily. When a creditor files an application for winding up of a company for recovery of a disputed debt, instead of instituting a suit against the debtor-company, he should ask himself why he is doing so. If he simply intends to escape the Court-fees, then, the consideration of paying less to the State revenue might ultimately be turned out to be a wrong option when he would find it difficult to prove insolvency of the company, for, 'commercial insolvency' is different from a 'temporary misfortune of a company'. And, when there is not even 'temporary misfortune of a company', not to speak of 'commercial insolvency', which has been the scenario of the instant case following its scrutinization, the winding up application is bound to fail. Therefore, it is always a better course to seek to have a Decree for a disputed debt and, thereafter, get it executed by the civil Court. After succeeding in civil suit, thus, the Decree-holder should not opt for executing the same through filing winding up application. Because, the said route may not be an easier one inasmuch as even after passing a Decree by a competent civil Court, the existence of a bona fide dispute is applicable to a decretal debt as well and capable of dispelling the fiction or presumption contained in section 242 of the Companies Act. The only difference is that the Decree against the alleged debtor raises a strong presumption that a genuine debt exists. The presumption can, however, be rebutted where there are substantial grounds for questioning the validity of the Decree. But, a debt simpliciter, which is not supported by a Judgment as evidence, has to be proved by other evidence. The difference lies not in the principle applicable but in the type of evidence produced to prove a debt and its effect. While this Court is of the view that a winding-up order may be a form of equitable execution, there is no equity in making such an order when the debt of the creditor is not in peril, although the substratum of the company may be gone, and when matters remain outstanding which can be best attended to in the interest of the share-holders by the company functioning as a company through its directors. It is trite law that a winding-up order is not a normal alternative in the case of a company to, the ordinary procedure for the realisation of debts due from it.</u>
36. The facts of the cases cited by the learned Advocate for the petitioner are completely different from the facts of the case in hand, for, in this case this Court finds bona fide dispute, whereas there was no bonafide dispute in the cases referred to and relied on by the learned Advocate for the petitioner-company; rather from the facts of the cases cited by the learned Advocate for the petitioner-company, it surfaces that the debts/demands made in those cases were either admitted or were denied merely to set up a defense to avoid the payments/debts.
37. In the premises above this Court does not have any option other than to dismiss this application without admitting it towards advertising the notice/information as to its admissio' by the Company Court.
38. To this end, let me take up issue No. 6, namely, whether, pursuant to issuance of Show Cause Notice by this Court upon the respondents, it is obligatory for this Court to admit the instant application towards its final disposal. For an effective adjudication of the issue, let me quote the provisions of section 249 of the Companies Act, which run as follows:
249. Powers of Court on hearing petition.—(1) On hearing the petition, the  Court may dismiss it with or without costs, or adjourn the hearing conditionally or unconditionally, or make any interim order or any other order which. it deems just, but the Court shall not refuse to make a winding up order on the ground only that the assets of the company have been mortgaged to an amount equal to, or in excess of, those assets or that the company has no assets.
(2) Where the petition is presented on the ground of default in filing the statutory report or in holding the statutory meeting the Court may order the costs to be paid by any persons who, in the opinion of the Court, are responsible for the default.
(3) Where the Court makes an order for the winding up of a company, it shall, except where a liquidator is appointed simultaneously, forthwith cause intimation thereof to be sent to the official receiver.
<u>39. From a plain reading of the provisions of section 249 of the Companies Act, it is easily understandable that once an application for winding up is presented, after hearing of the same, the Company Court has been invested with ample powers by section 249 of the Companies Act either to dismiss it outright with/without costs or to adjourn the hearing conditionally/unconditionally or pass any Order, including the Orders upon the respondents to show cause and interim Order. Further, Rule 63 of the Companies Rules dictates that—</u>
<u>‘........  at any time before the application has been advertised as directed, the Judge may alter the date so fixed for the hearing and instead of admitting the application for winding up the Judge may, in his discretion, direct that notice be given to the respondent company or its Board or to any relevant person to show cause why the application shall not be admitted; in such a case on cause shown, if any, the Judge may pass such Order as he deems fit.'</u>
<u>40. This Court, in consonance with the provisions of section 249 of the Companies Act and Rule 63 of the Companies Rules, usually does not order for admission of a winding up application directly when it is presented against a company which is a running concern with a solvent status and, particularly, when the Court comes to know that the respondent-company is a well-reputed company. In other words, since a winding-up petition is not a recognized mode for recovery of debt and if the company is shown to be solvent and the debt is bonafide disputed, the Company Court generally is reluctant to admit the petition.</u>
<u>41. Therefore, the power is conferred on the Company Court before whom the petition comes-up for admission to issue pre-admission notice to the company so that the company is not taken unaware and may appear and point out to the Company Court that the petitioner is actuated by an ulterior motive and presentation of the petition is a device to pressurise the company to submit to an unjust claim. It would, thus, not be wrong for the Company Court to perceive a winding up proceeding as a probable technique to recover money where a bonafide dispute is apparent, as there is an implied threat in them to bring disaster to the company, because an odium is also attached to such proceedings. In the case of Amalgamated Commercial Traders (P) Ltd. vs ACK Krishna-swami, MANU/SC/0369/1965,, the Supreme Court quoted with approval the following passage from Buckley on the Companies Acts (13th Ed. P. 451):</u>
<u>"A winding up petition is not a legitimate means of seeking to enforce payment of the debt which is bona fide disputed by the company. A petition presented ostensibly for a winding up order but really to exercise pressure will be dismissed, and under circumstances may be stigmatized as a scandalous abuse of the process of the Court. At one time petitions founded on disputed debt were directed to stand over till the debt was established by action. If, however, there was no reason to believe that the debt, if established, would not be paid, the petition was dismissed. The modern practice has been to dismiss such petitions. But, of course, if the debt is not disputed on some substantial ground, the Court may decide it on the petition and make the order."</u>
42. Therefore, the prayer made by the learned Advocate for the petitioner-company that this petition can be dismissed only after admitting the same, clearly overlooks various statutory safe-guards against admission, advertising and publication of winding-up petitions laid down in section 249 of the Companies Act and in the Companies Rules. While section 241 of the Companies Act sets out circumstances in which a company may be wound-up by the Court, one such being where the company is unable to pay its debts, section 242 of the Companies Act sets out the circumstances and situations in which a company may be deemed to be unable to pay its debts. Such a deeming fiction would arise where a notice is served upon the company making a demand of a debt exceeding Taka 500 then due and requiring the company to pay the same and the company has for a period of 3 (three) weeks neglected to pay the sum, or to secure or compound for it to the reasonable satisfaction of the creditor. Rule 62 of the Companies Rules provides that the petition for winding-up a company shall be presented to the Registry. Then comes Rule 63 which is very material. It provides that upon the filing of the petition, it shall be posted before the Company Court for admission of the petition and fixing a date for the hearing thereof and for the directions as to the advertisements to be published and the persons, if any, upon whom copies of the petition are to be served. The Court may, if it thinks fit, direct notice to be given to the company before giving directions as to the advertisement of the petition. It would appear that the Rule confers a discretionary power on the 'Company Court not to give any directions at that stage but merely issue a notice to the company before giving directions. If upon receipt of such notice, the company having appeared before the Company Court satisfies that the debt is bonafide disputed or the presentation of the petition is malafide actuated by an ulterior motive, or abuse of the process of the Court, certainly the Company Court may decline to admit the petition and may direct the party presenting the winding-up petition to prove its claim by a suit or any other manner.
43. In National Conduits P. Ltd. vs SS Arora 119671 37 Comp Case 786, the Supreme Court of India was considering the question whether a petition for winding-up cannot be placed for hearing before the Court unless the petition-is advertised. In that case, a Director of the company presented a petition in the High Court of Delhi under sections 433 and 439 of the Companies A.ct for an order of compulsory winding-up of the company; Notice of the petition was ordered to the company. The company filed an application that the winding-up petition filed by the director be dismissed and that the petition in the meantime not be advertised. The company petition was dismissed without advertisement on the ground that the proper remedy of the petitioner on the allegations of mismanagement of the affairs of the company and oppression of the minority shareholders was to file a petition under sections 397 and 398 of the Companies Act (for protection of minority shareholders) and the petition was instituted with a view to unfairly prejudice the interests of the shareholders of the company. After referring to Rules 24 and 96 of the Companies (Court) Rules, 1959 of India, the Supreme Court of India observed (at page 788):
A petition for winding-up cannot be placed for hearing before the court, unless the petition is advertised; that is clear from the terms of Rule 24(2). But that is not to say that as soon as the petition is admitted, it must be advertised. In answer to a notice to show cause why a petition for winding-up be not admitted, the company may show cause and contend that the filing of the petition amounts to an abuse of the process of the court. If the petition is admitted, it is still open to the company to move the court that in the interest of justice or to prevent abuse of the process of the court, the petition be not advertised. Such an application may be made where the court has issued notice under the last clause of Rule 96, and even when there is unconditional admission of the petition for winding-up. The power to entertain such an application of the company is inherent in the court, and Rule 9 of the Companies (Court) Rules, 1959, which reads: Nothing in these rules shall be deemed to limit or otherwise affect the inherent powers of the court to give such directions or pass such orders'as may be necessary for the ends of justice or to prevent abuse of the process of the Court.
44. In the case of Md Amin vs Bengal Shipping Line Ltd and others 60 DLR 444, the petitioner. one Md Amin filed an application under sections 241 and 242 read with section 245 of the Companies Act for winding up of the respondent-company (Bengal Shipping Line Limited) on the ground of ostensible non-payment of dividend and inability to partake of the profits. It was held by this Court that 'EVen admission of winding up application is to be granted sparingly and not as a rule. If the petitioner can show that he has no other remedy and that winding up is the only remedy available, he can come under section 241(vi), but that too only as a last resort and at the discretion of the Court.'
45. Therefore, this Court holds that even at the stage of entertaining the winding-up petition or admitting the winding-up petition or hearing the petition for winding up, the Company Court, to prevent the abuse of the process of the Court or to advance the cause of justice, may make such Order/Orders which are necessary to meet the ends of justice, including dismissing the winding up petition.
46. Since the present application for winding up of the respondent No. 1-company is not bona fide, and, also, given that the winding up of the respondent No. 1-company is not an appropriate remedy for the petitioner, as have been found by this Court hereinbefore, I am, thus, constrained to hold that this Court is not the proper forum for redressing the petitioner-company's grievance.
Accordingly, this winding up application is dismissed. However, there will be no Order as to costs.
End.
