full_judgment:
This Rule was issued, on 24-11-2020, calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the memo being No.08.01.0000.044.04.010.14/350 dated 16-11-2020 (annexure-A) issued by respondent No. 1 under signature of respondent No. 4 rejecting an application filed by the petitioner invoking the Proviso to section 160(1)(b) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984 (shortly, the 1984 Ordinance) seeking waiver from the required payment under that Proviso, as a condition precedent to filing reference application, shall not be declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect.
2. The facts of the case, as stated in the original reference application and in the subsequent supplementary affidavits, briefly, are that the petitioner is a charitable trust which is regularly filing its income tax returns within time for all the tax years. And, as part of its regular practice, tax returns for the assessment years/tax years 2011-2012 and 2012-2013 were filed with the Deputy Commissioner of Taxes (hereinafter referred to either as the DCT or the respondent No. 5) under section 75 of the 1984 Ordinance and assessed accordingly. Under the column 'net assets' of the petitioner, the assessment orders recorded that the petitioner received as donation from Grameen Telecom in the concerned income years and the said donation was not charged with income tax by the income tax authorities. Later on, the income tax returns of the petitioner were reopened under section 120 of the 1984 Ordinance by the Inspecting Joint Commissioner of Taxes (IJCT) who took a view that the -said donation does not fall within the purview of the exemption, because 'social business' is purportedly a business and not a charitable purpose and, then, directed the concerned Deputy Commissioner of Taxes (DCT) to assess the same as the income of the petitioner. Being aggrieved by the income tax authorities' above position, the petitioner filed appeals being Appeal Nos. 1042 & 1043/Coy.Circle-287/2018-2019 for the assessment years 2011-2012 and 2012-2013 before the Commissioner of Taxes (Appeals) who rejected the said appeals. Thereafter, the petitioner filed second appeal before the Taxes Appellate Tribunal under section 158 of the 1984 Ordinance. Since the petitioner was required to pay 10% of the difference for the two appeals i.e., Taka 1,76,26,378 and Taka 19,23,59,396 respectively under section 158(2) of the 1984 Ordinance, it made two applications addressing the Commissioner of Taxes praying for waiver from the payment requirement and, by a memo dated 8-5-2018, the Commissioner of Taxes reduced the amounts to Taka 25,00,000 and Taka 4,75,00,000 for the assessment years 2011-2012 and 2012-2013 respectively. However, after hearing the appeals, the same were dismissed by the Taxes Appellate Tribunal, Division Bench-I, Dhaka by order dated 5-3-2020.
3. Being aggrieved by the decision of the Taxes Appellate Tribunal, the petitioner took preparations to file reference applications under section 160(1) of the 1984 Ordinance. Since there is a requirement of making payment of 25% of the disputed amount under section 160(1)(b) of the 1984 Ordinance, the petitioner tiled a waiver application dated 29-7-2020 to the respondent Nos. 1 to 3 under the Proviso to section 160(1)(b) of the 1984 Ordinance stating, inter cilia, that the required payment was highly onerous for it, as the monies received by the petitioner had already been spent for charitable purposes in the form of social business and the petitioner at the then state was suffering from a severe disruptive effect on its activities. Pursuant thereto, the petitioner received a memo dated 20-9-2020 issued by respondent No. 1 under signature of respondent No. 4 permitting the petitioner to file reference applications under section 160(1) of the 1984 Ordinance, upon payment of Taka 4,15,52,444 and Taka 46,02,05,721 for the assessment years 2011-2012 and 2012-2013 respectively. Being aggrieved by the above, the petitioner filed a review application dated 4-10-2020 to the respondent No. 1 and, thereafter, made further representations dated 20-10-2020, which were never disposed of by the respondent No. 1. It is stated that the respondent No. 4, in the meanwhile, issued demand note dated 27-7-2020 under section 135 of the 1984 Ordinance even before expiry of 90 days limitation period for filing the reference application, against which the petitioner filed Writ Petition No. 4597 of 2020 and a Rule Nisi was issued with a stipulation that the same shall stand discharged on 31-10-2020 and the tax authorities may issue demand note only after 31-10-2020. Thereafter, on 2-11-2020 the respondent No. 5 issued a demand note for Taka 17,37,63,779 and Taka 197,70,91,219 for the assessment years 2011-2012 and 2012-2013 respectively. Under the circumstances, the petitioner filed Writ Petition No. 7243 of 2020 on 15-10-2020 impugning the order dated 20-9-2020, but this Court issued Rule on different terms _asking the tax authorities as to why they shall not be directed to dispose of the petitioner's representation dated 20-10-2020. Thereafter, the said Writ Petition No, 7243. of 2020 was non-prosecuted on 24-11-2020 as being infructuous as the representation dated 20-10-2020 was disposed of by the taxes authorities by an order dated 16-11-2020 which is impugned here in this Writ Petition. Hence, this Rule.
4. By filing an affidavit-in-opposition, the respondent No. 1 states, amongst others, that the petitioner in its application for waiver dated 29-77 2020 has simply stated that the requirement is `onerous' and 'monies received have already been spent' although at the relevant time the assessee had Taka 378,08,04,477 (Taka three hundreds seventy eight crores eight lacs four thousand four hundred and seventy seven) in its bank account which is absolutely contrary to the claim made in the application. In the review application filed by the assessee, it simply mentioned 'inability' to pay the statutory deposit without mentioning any reason as to why and how the petitioner is unable to pay the required amount despite having 6 to 7 times more money in its bank account.
5. Mr Mustafizur Rahman Khan, the learned Senior Advocate appearing for the petitioner-assessee, at the very outset, takes this Court through the waiver application dated 29-7-2020, the review application dated 4-10-2020 and the representation dated 20-10-2020, and submits that the impugned order dated 16-11-2020 has not discussed or taken into account any of the matters mentioned in the aforesaid applications in rejecting the petitioner's prayer for waiver from payment of the required amount in terms of section 160(1) of the 1984 Ordinance. He submits that in response to the petitioner's waiver application dated 29-7-2020, initially on 20-9-2020 an order was issued purporting to 'permit' filing of the reference application upon payment of the amount the petitioner was required to pay in any event if no waiver was accorded under the Proviso to section 160(1)(b) of the 1984 Ordinance. Subsequently, pursuant to filing of the Writ Petition No. 7243 of 2020 when the tax authorities were directed by this Court to dispose of the petitioner's further representation dated 20-10-2020 with reference to its waiver application, the petitioner's waiver application was rejected on 16-11-2020 by the respondent No. 1 in a whimsical and unreasonable manner in abuse of the power and through injudicious exercise of the discretion conferred upon it by the Proviso to section 160(1)(b) of the 1984 Ordinance, Mr Khan continues to submit. He also submits that the concerned respondent was not only obligated to consider the petitioner's prayer for waiver of payment, but it was incumbent upon the said respondent to state reasons in the event of rejection of the waiver-application. By placing annexures '1' and (Audit Reports and Financial Statements of the petitioner for the years ended on 30-6-2020 and 30-6-2021), he contends that the total liabilities of the petitioner are far more than the present Bank Balances and, thus, the 25% payment requirement is onerous for the petitioner. He submits that since the respondents have failed to state reasons for rejection of the petitioner's waiver application, the same is liable to be declared illegal. In an effort to substantiate his above submissions, the learned Senior Advocate for the petitioner has relied on a catena of case laws of our jurisdiction and those of foreign jurisdictions.
6. By making the above count of submissions, the learned Senior Advocate for the petitioner prays for making the Rule absolute.
7. Mr AM Amin Uddin, the learned Attorney-General, appearing for the respondent No. 1, refers to the Proviso to Clause (b) of sub-section (1) of section 160 of the 1984 Ordinance, and submits that the issue of waiver is absolutely discretionary on the part of the respondent No. 1 inasmuch as the Legislature has purposefully employed the word 'may' in the said Proviso. He then places the provisions of section 194 of the Customs Act, 1969, and submits that the language of the Proviso to section 160(1)(b) of 1984 Ordinance unlike section 194 of the Customs Act does not require the respondent to even consider `undue hardship' nor does it require to state any reason for rejecting or allowing such application. Mr AM Amin Uddin next submits that although the Proviso to section 160(1)(b) of the 1984 Ordinance does not require to state any reason while disposing of the application for waiver, such applications are never disposed of whim-sically; rather all the facts and circumstances are usually taken into consideration at the time of such disposal and, accordingly, in issuing the impugned memo the respondents have taken into account the petitioner's financial capacity as reflected in its bank account. He argues that since this assessee has already availed complete waiver of Taka 25,00,000 and Taka 4,75,00,000 at the time of filing appeals before the Appellate Tribunal, the respondents did not find it appropriate to waive the payment required for filing reference application and, hence, there is no scope to say that the waiver application was not disposed of without considering, any reason. By placing the letter dated 3-12-2023 issued by the respondent No. 4 (annexure-Y), the learned Attorney-General submits that in the midst of hearing when this Court verbally directed the tax authorities to furnish the detailed reasons for rejecting the petitioner's waiver application, the tax authorities have complied with it by issuance of the aforesaid letter and, therefore, after receiving the same the petitioner ought to have non-prosecuted this case without wasting further time. The learned Attorney-General lastly submits that the facts of the cases referred to by the learned Advocate for the petitioner are different and, therefore, the 'ratios' laid down in the cited cases are not applicable here in this case.
8. By putting forward the above submissions, the learned Attorney-General for the respondent No.1 prays for discharging the Rule with exemplary costs.
9. Upon hearing the learned Advocate for the petitioner and the learned Attorney-General, on perusal of the petitioner's application as well as the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the respondent Nos. 1 and 4 together with their annexures and having read the relevant statutory laws and case laws cited from the various Law Journals, it appears to this Court that the only issue to be adjudicated upon by this Court is whether the concerned respondent, namely, National Board of Revenue (respondent No. I) is duty bound to state reason's while it rejects an application filed under the Proviso to Clause (b) of sub-section (1) of section 160 of the 1984 Ordinance.
10. In quest for the answer to the question posed hereinbefore, it would be useful if the entire provisions of sub-section (1) of section 160 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 1984 (as they were at the relevant time of passing the impugned Order on 16-11-2020) are quoted which run as follows;
160. Reference to the High Court Division.-
(1) The assessee or the Commissioner may, within ninety days from the date of receipt of the order of the Appellate Tribunal communicated to him under section 159, by application in the prescribed form, accompanied, in the case of an application by the assessee, by a fee of two thousand taka, refer to the High Court Division any question of law arising out of such order. Provided that no reference under sub-section (1) shall lie against an order of the Taxes Appellate Tribunal, unless the assessee has paid the following tax at the rate of-
(a) fifteen per cent of the difference between the tax as determined on the basis of the order of the Taxes Appellate Tribunal and the tax payable under section 74 where tax demand does not exceed.one million taka;
(b) twenty five per cent of the difference between the tax as determined on the basis of the order of the Taxes Appellate Tribunal and the tax payable under section 74 where tax demand exceeds one trillion taka:
Provided further that the Board may, on an application made in this behalf, modify or' waive, in any case, the requirement of such payment.
<u>11. From a plain reading of the aforequoted provisions of law, it appears to this Court that the power of the National Board of Revenue (respondent No. 1) to waive the required payment for filing a reference application is completely a discretionary one as the Legislature has employed the word 'may' in the Proviso to Clauses (a) and (b) of sub-section (1) of section 160 of the 1984 Ordinance and, more so, when the law does not prescribe any consequence for non-consideration of an application for waiver of such payment, there is hardly any scope for this Court to see this Proviso as a mandatory one.</u>
12. The question, however, has been raised by the learned Senior Advocate for the petitioner is that — while it is a discretionary power of the National Board of Revenue either to allow or reject a waiver application filed under the Proviso to Clauses (a) and (b) of section 160(1) of the 1984 Ordinance, it is mandatory for them to furnish reason's for rejecting an application under the aforesaid Proviso of section 160(1) of the 1984 Ordinance.
13. Let us embark upon examination of the said issue. It is not unknown to all that in course of discharging the duties by the functionaries of the State or officials of a local authority, that is to say, the executives of Bangladesh, they are at times required to conduct the functions of a quasi-judicial nature. And, in that event, the executives are legally duty bound to state reason's in passing any decision or order. Even during serving purely as an executive, it may be incumbent upon the concerned executive to state reasonls in passing a decision or order, based on the peculiar facts and circumstances of the matter under consideration.
14. Evidently, the order impugned here in this case is an administrative order; not a judicial or quasi-judicial order. Since the executives are required to pass order/s judiciously containing reasonings even in course of carrying out a purely administrative work if the facts and circumstances so warrant, let us see whether in passing the instant impugned Order, the concerned executive (tax authorities) took into consideration the pertinent facts and circumstances placed by the applicant before the concerned executive authority, namely, National Board of Revenue (respondent No. 1).
15. Mr Mustafizur Rahman Khan, the learned Senior Advocate for the petitioner, by citing the cases of Ayman Textile and Hosiery Ltd vs Government of Bangladesh and others (an unreported Judgment passed on 24-7-2022 in Writ Petition No. 11087 of 2021), R vs Ministry of Defence ex.p Murray [1998] COD 134, Gautam vs The Union of India (U01). (1993) 1 SCC 78, The Siemens Engineering & Manufacturing Co. of India Ltd vs The Union of India (UOI) and others AIR 1976 SC 1785, AK Kraipak and others vs Union of India (UOI) and others AIR 1970 SC 150, has endeavored to make out a case that the very purpose of incorporation of the Proviso to Clauses (a) and (b) of section 160(1) of the 1984 Ordinance is to enable an applicant to file a reference application and, therefore, the concerned respondents were obligated to consider the petitioner's application for waiver of the payment required under the Proviso to section 160(1) of the 1984 Ordinance positively, so that because of a petitioner's financial hardship, the forum/s created by the Legislature by a special piece of legislation for filing a reference application before the High Court Division does not become unreachable or unavailable.
16. Let us now judge and determine the legality and propriety of the impugned order on the touchstone of the ratios laid down in the cases referred to by the learned Senior Advocate Mr Mustafizur Rahman Khan.
17. In the Judgment dated 24-7-2022 in the case of Ayman Textile and Hosiery Ltd. vs Government of Bangladesh and others [passed in Writ Petition No. 11087 of 2021 (unreported)], the Rule was issued in the following terms; Let a Rule Nisi be issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the order dated 9-8-2021 passed by the respondent No. 2, Customs, Excise and VAT Appellate Tribunal in the CEVT/Case (Customs)-336/2021 directing the petitioner to deposit 15% of the duty demanded and penalty imposed through treasury chalan and 15% of the same through unconditional bank guarantee without considering the undue hardship caused to the Petitioner (Annexure-1-2) and the subsequent order dated 12-10-2021 passed by the Respondent No. 2 rejecting the CEVT/Case (Cus)-33612021 (Annexure-J) on failure of the Petitioner to comply with above order in depositing 15% of the duty demanded and penalty imposed through treasury chalan and 15% of the same through unconditional bank guarantee due to undue hardship should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and are of no legal effect and as to why the Respondent No. 2 should not be directed to reconsider the hardship application, if any, filed by the Petitioner in accordance with law, and accordingly, admit the CEVT/Case (Customs) 336/2021 and/or pass such other or further Order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.
18. About the aforecited case, it is the interpretative position of the learned Senior Advocate for the petitioner that the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh observed that the Tribunal passed the order in response to the hardship application in a mechanical and slipshod manner as tantamount to unreasonably and injudiciously penalising the petitioner without adequate reason; that the Court further observed in the aforesaid case that the question of undue hardship inextricably merges with an initial satisfaction of the prima facie merits of the petitioner's case and, according to the Court, relaxing albeit partially the exacting pre-conditions for filing an appeal, but without reason for such relaxation and as also being devoid of citation of grounds that in the appellate authority's view militate against the granting an unconditional and total waiver in the alternative, is found to be inherently bad in law and must be set-aside.
<u>19. And, on the afore-cited case of Ayman Textile the arguments of the learned Attorney-General are that the above-mentioned decision deals with the issue of waiver under section 194 of the Customs Act, which requires the authority to dispense with the requirement of statutory deposit if the authority is satisfied that the requirement will cause 'undue hardship' to the importer. Unlike section 194 of the Customs Act, Proviso to Clauses (a) and (b) of section 160(1) of the 1984 Ordinance does not require any particular situation such as 'undue hardship' or others to be satisfied. The language of section 194 of the Customs Act and that of Proviso to Clauses (a) and (b) of section 160 of the 1984 Ordinance and their approach are completely different, inasmuch as while section 194 of the Customs Act has limited and confined its discretion to situation of 'undue hardship' of the importer but the Proviso to Clauses (a) and (b) of section 160(1) of the 1984 Ordinance has taken a wider approach as to which issue can or cannot be considered by the National Board of Revenue while keeping the matter completely discretionary. As such the ratio of the afore-cited Ayman Textile case is distinguishable on law and facts as well, and is not applicable to the cases involving application under the Proviso to Clauses (a) and (b) of section 160(1) of the 1984 Ordinance.</u>
20. Citing the case of R vs Ministry of Defence ex.p Murray 11998] COD 134, the learned Senior Advocate Mr Mustafizur Rahman Khan submits that in the said case the Court laid down eleven principles and one of them is although the law did not recognise a general duty to give reasons, they should be given if justice could not be achieved in the absence of reasons.
21. In response to the aforecited English case, the learned Attorney-General submits that when a Court-Martial sentenced the accused without stating any reason in its verdict, the above principle was rightly laid down, for no judicial or quasi-judicial body can pass any verdict without assigning any reason. Since in this case, the decision is purely an administrative one, there is no obligation on the part of the concerned executive to state any reason. In an endeavour to make out persuasive case, the learned Senior Advocate Mr Mustafizur Rahman Khan refers to a few Indian case laws, and submits that in the case of Gautam vs UOL (1993) 1 SCC 78, the Indian Supreme Court observed that where a statute requires reasons to be given, failure to give reasons will render the decision liable to be set-aside.
22. In reply thereto, the learned Attorney-General's arguments are that the observations of the Court in Gautam vs UOL (1993) only applies to situations where the decision was not backed by any reason despite reasons being required by the statute itself. Proviso to Clauses (a) and (b) of section 160(1) of the 1984 Ordinance does not require the National Board of Revenue to provide any reason for allowing or rejecting any application under the said Proviso to section 160 and, as such, the said case is irrelevant to the instant facts and circumstances.
23. By referring to the case of the Siemens Engineering & Manufacturing Co. of India Ltd. vs The Union of India (UOI) and others (AIR 1976 SC 1785), the learned Senior Advocate for the petitioner professes that it is a settled principle of law that where an authority makes an order in exercise of a quasi-judicial function, it must record its reason in support of the order it makes. Every quasi-judicial order must be supported by reasons.
24. On the other hand, the learned Attorney-General submits that the aforequoted decision of the Supreme Court of India as reported in AIR 1976 SC 1785 applies only to the order/decision which is quasi-judicial in nature and hence must be backed by reasons. But the decision in question given by the National Board of Revenue under the Proviso to Clauses (a) and (b) of section 160(1) is not quasi-judicial in nature, rather the same is delivered in the capacity of a purely administrative functionary and, as such, the same is not required to be backed by reasons.
25. By placing the case of AK Kraipak and others vs Union of India (UOI) and others (AIR 1970 SC 150), Mr Mustafizur Rahman Khan submits that the Supreme Court of India held that the power exercised by selection board is an administrative power and test validity of selections. The Court further observed that the distinction between administrative power and quasi-judicial power is becoming increasingly blurred; that to determine the nature of a given power, one must consider the power itself, the individuals it is granted to, the legal framework, the consequences of its exercise, and the expected manner of its execution; that the concept of quasi-judicial power has evolved over time, with powers once deemed administrative now being viewed as quasi-judicial; that the purpose of natural justice rules is to ensure justice and prevent miscarriages of justice; that these rules supplement valid law and have evolved over time - no one should be a judge in his own case and no decision should be given without affording a reasonable hearing; that additional principles include holding quasi-judicial inquiries in good faith, without bias, and not arbitrarily; that while it was previously believed that natural justice applied only when an authority was required to act judicially, this limitation is now challenged; that the rules should not be inapplicable to administrative inquiries, as both aim for a just decision; that the distinction between administrative and quasi-judicial inquiries is not always clear, and unjust decisions in administrative inquiries can have significant consequences.
26. The learned Attorney-General's reply on the aforecited decision (AIR 1970 SC 150) is that as per the Indian Supreme Court, a decision of selection should be based on reason. It is his argument that the said decision applies to situations where there are Limited posts to be filled and some candidates are selected and some are not. Therefore, according to the learned Attorney-General, this decision is also not applicable as being distinguishable. In the cited case, not being selected for the post implies many reasons amongst which one is that selected candidates are expected to be holding better qualifications than the others and, as such, there is an issue of comparison between the qualifications of those who are and are not selected. The learned Attorney-General argues that it would not be wrong to say that the qualities of other candidates are the reason for not being selected. In such circumstances it is quite expected that the authorities would be required to provide reasons for not selecting a candidate. Unlike the cited case in the instant writ petition the decision of the respondent is neither dependent on the comparative position of all the other applications filed under the relevant provisions of law nor acceptance of the applications being limited to any number or condition, the authorities cannot be compelled to provide any reason while applying its discretion. Hence the instant cited case is not applicable to the present situation.
27. This Court has minutely gone through all the aforecited cases in an effort to learn the ratios laid down therein. While this Court finds that the facts and law of the case cited by the learned Senior Advocate for the petitioner from our jurisdiction (Ayman Textile and Hosiery Ltd vs Government of Bangladesh) being not similar is not relevant for adjudication of the present case, the ratios laid down in the case laws of foreign jurisdictions, albeit the same are not binding on us and are merely persuasive, have not derived from the interpretation of the similar provisions of the income tax laws.
28. As of now, there was no occasion for either of the Divisions of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh to interpret the Proviso to Clauses (a) and (b) of section 160(1) of the 1984 Ordinance towards laying down the appropriate principles on the issue that following receiving an application under the aforesaid Proviso to section 160(1) of the 1984 Ordinance, whether the National Board of Revenue is legally bound to state reason/s while it rejects the said application. In the case of Messers Hyundai Corporation vs National Board of Revenue 2001 BLD (AD) 55, when the High Court Division summarily rejected the Writ Petition filed by the assessee challenging the decision of the National Board of Revenue rejecting the prayer for waiving 25% of the required payment for filing reference application, the aforesaid Order of the High Court Division was affirmed. In the aforecited case, the High Court Division rejected the Writ Petition on the ground that since waiver of the required payment for filing a reference application is a discretionary power endowed upon the National Board of Revenue, no illegality was committed. However, the Hon'ble Appellate Division dismissed the Civil Petition for leave to Appeal (thereby rejecting the Writ Petition) on the ground that the writ petition was not maintainable as it was not founded on the violation of any fundamental rights or any legal right of the petitioner.
29. Usually, the executives are not required to pass any detailed order in carrying out their routine works. However, if a law prescribes an appellate forum in case of being aggrieved by an order or decision of an executive, the said order/decision must be a speaking one. It is the considered view of this Court that when any person, be it a natural person or a juristic person, files any application to a State-Functionary or to an official of a local authority agitating any legal or equitable issue, it is incumbent upon the concerned Government authority to dispose of the same at its earliest convenience by giving a speaking order/decision containing reasonings therein, so that if the applicant is aggrieved s/he may decide as to whether it is worthy of challenging before the higher authority or before any competent forum or taking any other recourse of law, if there be any.
30. It has been contended 'by the learned Attorney-General that while the tax authorities are not legally bound to notify an applicant under the Proviso to Clauses (a) and (b) of section 160(1) of the 1984 Ordinance, however, in this case, the respondent No. 1 (National Board of Revenue) disposed of the petitioner's waiver application by giving its decision on 1641-2020 in writing. It is the practice of all the Government authorities of Bangladesh, in particular the revenue department, to dispose of any application by passing appropriate order/decision, the learned Attorney-General claims. Moreso, during the hearing of the instant case before this Court, when the petitioner requested for supplying detailed reasons for rejection of its waiver application, the National Board of Revenue provided the reasons for rejecting the waiver application instantly without squandering any time. Learned Attorney-General contends that had the petitioner asked for the reasons in writing to the respondents, they would have supplied the same long ago. Instead of doing that the petitioner, at first, filed review application on 4-10-2020 and, thereafter, filed another application for reviewing the respondent's decision. The learned Attorney-General submits that there is no provision in the law for reviewing the decision given by the National Board of Revenue under the Proviso to Clauses (a) and (b) of section 160(1) of the 1984 Ordinance. He alleges that the petitioner is employing all these devices merely for delaying the payment of taxes assessed by the DCT pursuant to reopening the petitioner's tax files for the assessment years 2011-2012 and 2012-2013 by the MT, which later on was affirmed by the two successive appellate fora.
31. From the examination of the events that took place in dealing with the petitioner's tax files for the assessment years 2011-2012 and 2012-2013, it transpires that the petitioner's above mentioned tax files were reopened on 31-10-2013 by the IJCT invoking section 120 of the 1984 Ordinance, pursuant to which the concerned DCT assessed the appropriate tax to be paid by the petitioner. Against which the petitioner then filed appeal to the Commissioner of Taxes (Appeal), which was rejected. Thereafter when the petitioner preferred second appeal, the National Board of Revenue reduced the required payment under section 160(1 )(a) of the 1984 Ordinance to only Taka 25,00,000 from the required payment of Taka 1,76,26,378 for the assessment year 2011-2012 and to Taka 4,75,00,000 from the required payment of Taka 19,23,59,396 for the assessment year 2012-2013. Thereafter, since the time of passing the decision and order by the Tribunal on 5-3-2020, a considerable length of time elapsed, but no reference application has been filed as of now on the plea of not getting the reasonis for rejection of the petitioner's waiver application, which the respondents have supplied immediately after asking for the same during the hearing. And, in fact, during hearing of this Writ Petition it was the position of the petitioner that if the petitioner receives the reasonls for rejecting its waiver application, the instant Rule will be non-prosecuted by the petitioner. But the petitioner took a U-turn after receiving the letter dated 3-12-2023 containing the details for rejection of the petitioner's waiver application, pertinent portions of which are quoted below:
“আদিষ্ট হয়ে উপযুক্ত বিষয় ও সূত্রের প্রতি মহোদয়ের সদয় দৃষ্টি আকর্ষণ করছি?
বিষয়ে বর্ণিত করদাতা গ্রামীণ টেলিকম ট্রাস্ট এর আয়কর অধ্যাদেশ ১৯৮৪ এর ১৬০(১) ধারার প্রোভাইসো অনুযায়ী আবেদনের Waiver প্রেক্ষিতে প্রদান না করার কারণ সমূহ আপনার সদয় অবগতির জন্য নিম্নে উল্লেখ করা হলো:
(ক) করদাতা গ্রামীণ টেলিকম ট্রাস্ট কর্তৃক দায়ের এর পূর্বে কর কমিশনার, কর অঞ্চল-১৪, ঢাকা কর্তৃক আয়কর অধ্যাদেশ, ১৯৮৪ এর ১৫৮২) ধারার প্রোভাইসো অনুযায়ী ২০১১-২০১২ করবর্ষের জন্য টা: ২৫,০০,০০০ এবং ২০১২-২০১৩ করবর্ষের জন্য টা: ৪,৭৫,০০,০০০ ৬/৪1%০1 প্রদান করা হয়েছিল? যার আদেশ নং-৬৫২০)/ক:অ:-১৪/ওয়েভার/২০১৭-২০১৮/৭৪ তাং-৫-৫-২০১৮ খিঃ?
(খ) কর কমিশনারের কার্যালয় কর অঞ্চল-১৪, ঢাকা এর পত্র নথি নং- ৬৫২)/ক অ-১৪/ওয়েভার/ ২০২০-২০২১/১৪৩ তারিখ: ৮-৯-২০২০ইং পর্যালোচনায় প্রতীয়মান হয় যে, করদাতা গ্রামীণ গ্রামীন টেলিকম ট্রাস্ট এর কর প্রদানের আর্থিক সামর্থ্য এবং স্বচ্ছলতা রয়েছে। করদাতার ২০৯৯-২০২০ করবর্ষের নিরীক্ষিত হিসাব বিবরণী অনুযায়ী এফডিআর ক্রয়ে বিনিয়োগের পরিমাণ টা: ৩৭৮,০৮১০৪,৪ ৭৭ এবং নগদ ও ব্যাংক স্থিতি টা: ৯,৯৩৭৭,১৮৫?
<u>32. From the above-quoted portions of the letter dated 3-12-2023 issued by the National Board of Revenue, it is vividly evident that the concerned respondents have given their reasonings, upon taking the circumstances of the petitioner into their consideration. Since in this case, the petitioner's only grievance is that it has not been provided with the grounds for rejection of the application for waiver of the required payment for filing a reference application and, evidently, the same having been supplied by the National Board of Revenue, this Court does not see any further cause or grievance of the petitioner to be adjudicated upon by it. Hence, this Court finds the stance taken by the petitioner is an abuse of the process of the Court and the allegation raised by the learned Attorney-General that since the Tribunal's verdict on 5-3-2020, instead of filing any reference application or paying the tax, the petitioner is purposefully delaying the payment appears to this Court to be true. It is a trite law that the writ jurisdiction being an equitable forum cannot be availed of by a person who comes with unclean hands. And, on this score only, the present Rule is liable to be discharged.</u>
33. It appears from the Proviso to Clauses (a) and (b) of section 160(1) of the 1984 Ordinance that passing an Order under the aforesaid Proviso by the National Board of Revenue is a function of an administrative nature and, accordingly, the National Board of Revenue simply informed the petitioner that it had rejected the petitioner's waiver application by the impugned order dated 16-11-2020 in which this Court does not find any illegality. And, moreso, latterly when the above-quoted details were supplied by the National Board of Revenue and, the same having been merged with the impugned order, there remains no room for any ordinary person, let alone for this Court, to see any illegality or infirmity in the impugned order.
The Rule is, thus, discharged without any Order as to costs.
End.

Monoranjan Pal and others ……..Appellants
VS
Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Narayangonj and others ……..Respondents
full_judgment:
Hasan Foez Siddique, CJ: The appellants filed Title Suit No.21 of 2000 in the Second Court of Joint District Judge, Narayangonj for declaration of title in respect of the suit described in the schedule to the plaint stating, inter alia, that one Chandra Mohon Pal and Modon Mohon Pal were the CS recorded tenants having 0.55 acre of -land of CS plot No.12 appertaining to CS khatian No.17 of Mouza Alinagar under Police Station-Fatullah, District Narayangonj. Chandra Mohon Pal died leaving behind one daughter, plaintiff No.1 who inherited 8 annas shares of the suit land. Modon Mohon Pal also died leaving behind his daughter Sattya Bala Pal who married with one Ramani Mohon Pal. Sattya Bala Pal died leaving behind 6 sons including plaintiff Nos.2 and 3 who inherited the remaining portion of the suit property. During SA operation their names had been duly recorded in SA khatian. One of the sons of Sattya Bala Pal, namely, Chitta Ranjan Pal died and whereabouts of 3 other sons were not known. The plaintiff Nos.2-3 had been owning and possessing the respective shares of their brothers including their own shares of the suit property. Suit land was residential plot of the plaintiffs which had been let out to other persons on rent for bricks and stones business. They had paid rents and taxes to the government upto 1392 BS. After the war of liberation, the plaintiffs have .been residing at their present addresses in Jamalpur and Narayangonj. Due to absence of the plaintiffs, the suit land had been wrongly recorded in RS khatian No.4 in the name of the government. The government mutated the suit land in the name of M/s Elahi Buksh Cold Storage and Company Limited (in short, the Company) represented by the Ministry of Commerce, the Government of Bangladesh in Mutation Case No.4884 of 1991. Cause of action of the suit arose on 2-1-2000 when the plaintiffs went to the concerned office for payment of rent and came to know about the said wrong record of right. So, they instituted the present suit.
2. The defendant Nos.1-3 and 5-6 contested the suit by filing separate sets of written statements. The defendant Nos.1-3 contended that the suit land being abandoned property had been recorded in RS khatian No.4 during the last revisional survey operation and was amalgamated with other plots of Elahi Buksh Cold Storage & Company Limited measuring 1.92 acres of land in the name of the Ministry of Commerce, Government of Bangladesh in Miscellaneous Case No.7/85 (AP) dated 5-12-1985. The Company had paid land development Tax upto 1405 BS. The plaintiffs, forging some documents, instituted the present suit with a view to grab the government property.
3. The contentions of the defendant Nos.5 and 6 in short, are that the suit land measuring 55 decimals were recorded in the names of the plaintiffs and others in SA khatian No.21, SA Plot No-12- Plaintiff No.1, Taru Bala Pal sold 0.14 acre of land from suit plot to the defendant Nos.5 and 6, the Company by registered sale deed No.5323 dated 29-9-62. Rukkoni Bala and others sold 0.16 acre of land of suit plot by registered sale deed No.6807 dated 6-12-62 to the company. Mohon Razbonshi sold out 0.12 acre of land by registered deed No.731 dated 25-1-1963 to the Company. Aeson Company Limited, by deed No.4401 dated 12-6-1999, exchanged 14 decimals of land with the Company. The defendant no.5, while enjoying the possession of the suit land, established a cold storage therein. During the war of liberation the original owenrs of the company left the country. Accordingly, vide SET Miscellaneous Case No.7/85(AP) dated 5-12-85 the suit properties had been declared as abandoned property and it was ultimately vested in the government. Its management had been controlled by the Board of management duly constituted by Ministry of Commerce. During RS survey the suit property had been duly recorded in the name of the Government of Bangladesh represented by the Ministry of Commerce. The said khatian had been amalgamated with other properties of the company measuring 1.92 acres of land and was finally published in RS khatian No.4. The plaintiff never possessed the suit land and that the instant suit had been instituted by the plaintiffs in order to grab the government property with some fictitious documents. The suit was liable to be dismissed with costs.
4. The trial Court decreed the suit. The Government preferred appeal and the appellate Court dismissed the appeal thereby affirmed the judgment and decree of the trial Court. Then the Government filed Civil Revision No. 4554 of 2008 in the High Court Division and obtained Rule. The High Court Division, by the impugned judgment and order dated 24-1-2010, made the said Rule absolute. Thus, the plaintiffs have preferred this appeal upon getting leave.
5. Mr Nozrul Islam Chowdhury, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the appellants, submits that the High Court Division has committed an error of law in dismissing the suit reversing the concurrent findings of facts holding that the instant suit was not maintainable. He further submits that all the three Courts below concurrently found the plaintiffs' possession in the suit land and that the plaintiffs have been able to prove their title in the suit land, the High Court Division most illegally dismissed the suit inasmuch as the plaintiffs acquired valid title in the suit land by way of inheritance.
6. Mr Amit Das Gupta, learned Deputy Attorney General appearing for the respondent Government, submits that the High Court Division upon proper appreciation of the materials on record, held that the instant suit was not maintainable. He submits that the plaintiffs have failed to prove their title and possession in the entire suit land, the High Court Division rightly dismissed the suit.
7. Admittedly, the suit land originally belonged to Chandra Mohon Pal and Madon Mohon Pal to the extent of 8 annas share each. Chandra Mohon Pal died leaving only daughter, Taru Bala Pat, the plaintiff No.1. On the other hand, Modon Mohon Pal died leaving daughter Sattya Bala Pal. Sattya Bala Pal died leaving 6(six) sons, namely, Chitta Ranjan Pal, Monoranjan Pal, Shishu Ranjan Pal, Khushi Ranjan Pal, Nidhon Ranjan Pal and Aurun Ranjan Pal. Khusi Ranjan Pal, Nidon Ranjan and Aurun Ranjan Pal were untraced since 1971 and their interest was ultimately devolved to their brothers Monoronjan Pal and Shishu Ranjan Pal, the plaintiff No.2 and 3. SA record-of-rights was prepared in their names.
8. It was the case of the contesting defendants that Taru Bala and others transferred 0.14 acre of land on 29-9-1962, Rukkhini Bala and others transferred their 0.16 acre of land on 6-12-1962 and Mohon Rajbonshi transferred 0.12 acre of land on 25-1-1963 to M/s Elahi Boksh and Company Limited. From the materials on record, it appears that the plaintiffs are the successive heirs of CS recorded tenants and their names were duly recorded in SA khatian. The contesting defendants relied upon 3(three) kabala deeds. Of them, kabla deed dated 6-12-1962 in respect of 0.16 acre of land was executed by Rukkhini Bala and others and kabala deed dated 25-1-1963 in respect of 0.12 acre of land was executed by Mohon Rajbongshi. The defendants hopelessly failed to prove the source of title of Rukkhini Bala and Mohon Rajbongshi. In absence of any proof of source of title of the executants of those deeds, it is difficult to hold that the defendants had acquired any title on the basis of deeds dated 6-12-1962 and 25-1-1963. The learned Advocate appearing for the respondents also failed to satisfy us as to the source of their title. In such view of the matter, it is difficult to hold that by those deeds, the contesting defendants have acquired any title in the suit land. In such circumstances, we have no hesitation to hold that the plaintiffs' title in the suit land remained undisturbed. The Court of facts below concurrently disbelieved the execution and registration of the said deeds.
9. All the Courts below concurrently found the plaintiff's possession in the suit land. It is relevant here to state the finding of the High Court Division as to possession of the suit land. It held, "as to possession of the plaintiffs opposite parties the findings of the trial Court as well as the appellate Court being passed on evidence on detail discussion I found no reason to interfere with."
<u>10. It is settled principle that possession may prima-facie raise a presumption of title. If at any time a person with title was in possession of the property, the law allows the presumption that such possession was in continuation of the title vested in him. The accepted proposition law is that possession follows title. Presumption of possession over an open land always is deemed to be that of the owner unless it is proved that he is a trespasser. In the eye of law an owner would be deemed to be in possession of a property so long as there is no intrusion.</u>
11. Considering the facts and circumstances, we are of the view that the High Court Division committed an error of law in not holding that the plaintiffs have been able to prove their title and possession in the suit land. 12. Accordingly, we find the substance in this appeal. Thus, the appeal is allowed. The judgment and order dated 24-1-2010 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.4554 of 2008 is hereby set-aside.
End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 22nd day of January, 2012 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.4687 of 2000)
full_judgment:
M. Enayetur Rahim, J: This civil petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 22-1-2012 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.4687 of 2000 discharging the Rule.
2. The relevant facts leading to the filing of the leave petition, in brief, are as follows: The predecessor of the present respondents instituted Title Suit No.259 of 1995 in the Court of Sub- ordinate Judge, First Court, Dhaka for declaration of title over the suit land, and that the purchase deed of the defendant No.1 (present petitioner) dated 21-6-1988 is not binding upon her. Eventually, the said suit was transferred to the Court of Sub-ordinate Judge and Artha Rin Adalat No.3, Dhaka and renumbered as Title Suit No.101 of 1997 (General).
3. In the plaint averments have been made, inter alia, that the suit land measuring 4 decimal with tin-shed structure appertaining to CS Plot No.6, SA Plot No.2511, CS Khatian No. 6362, SA Khatian No.1509 of Mouza Shahar, Dhaka, thereafter Wan, Police Station Sutrapur, Dhaka, originally belonged to Hariprasad Bandhapadhaya, Bhuban Mukhapdhaya, Omrita Lal Mukhapadhaya and Shashibala Devi and their names were correctly recorded in CS Khatian No.6362. After the death of Hariprashad Bandhapadhaya, Surendra Nath Bandhapahaya became the owner and possessor of the land by amicable partition among the heirs of Haribrashad Bandha-padhaya. The father of the plaintiff was a servant under Hariprashad Bandhapadhaya. In that connection, she was residing along with her family members in a portion of the suit plot. Surendranath Bandhapadhaya settled the suit property by Amalnama on 15-9-1350 BS and made over the possession of the land to the plaintiff. Plaintiff had possessed the land peacefully by paying rent to the Zaminder and constructed a tin-shed building thereon, thereafter connected gas, water and electric service. The plaintiff was an illiterate woman and her sons were minor during the operation of SA record. She had no knowledge about survey. The SA record was prepared in the name of Dhakeshawari Cotton Mills Limited. But, they had never been in the possession of the suit land. The plaintiff has been trying to institute a suit for rectification of SA Khatian. In the meantime, revisional Survey started in Dhaka City. The plaintiff applied for mutation of the suit land in the office of Assistant Commissioner (Land) on 25-7-1995. The Assistant Commissioner (Land) instructed orally her for taking appropriate step in the Court. A few officers of defendant No.1 disclosed on 19-10-1995 that they have purchased the land from liquidator on behalf of Dhakeshawari Cotton Mills Limited on 21-6-1988 vide deed No.1618 and they threatened her to handover the vacant possession. The plaintiff collected the certified copy of the said deed. The said deed clouded the right, title and interest of the plaintiff. Hence the plaintiff filed the suit.
4. The defendant No.1, present petitioner contested the suit by a filing written statement denying all the material statements made in the plaint contending, inter alia that, the suit is barred by defence of Pakistan Ordinance, East Pakistan Government and Local Authority (Land and Building), 1970 and Article 10 of President Order No.27 of 1972. All the affairs of Dhakeshawari Cotton Mills Limited had been declared 'Enemy' in 1965 and made over all activities of the firm to the erstwhile East Pakistan Industrial Development Corporation by Gazette notification on 6-9-1965. Gopinath Poddar was not the Zamindar of the suit holding along with holding No.37, Hatkhola Road, Dhaka. The successor of Gopinath Poddar namely, who is subsequent purchasers Shree Narendranath Bandha Padhaya, Shree Dhiurendnath Bandhapadhaya, Shree Birendranath Bandhapadhaya, all sons of late Hariprasad Bandapadhaya and Amarendra Nath Bandhapadhaya, Shree Sattandra Nath Bandhapadhaya transferred the entire suit plot to Dhakeshawari Cotton Mills Limited by registered deed on 6-10-1953 (19-6-1350 BS) The name of Dhakeshwari Cotton Mills Limited had been correctly recorded in the SA Khatian. The husband of the plaintiff who subsequently substituted as plaintiff No.7 was an employee of East Pakistan Industrial Development Corporation and in that connection, a flat of the suit property allotted to him for residential purpose. The plaintiff No.7 and his wife and other plaintiffs have been possession the flat since 1966. The plaintiff No.7 had been paying rent of the flat from his salary to the defendant No.1 and he was retired from service in the year 1993. The plaintiff No.7 filed various suits including Title Suit No.25 of 199.5 only to harass the defendant No.1 in view of defeat the eviction proceeding of the petitioner. He filed suit for a declaration that he was the legal and bonafide possessor of the suit property. The petition under Order 39 Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, had been rejected by the concerned court on 13-8-1995, thereafter, plaintiff, the wife of plaintiff Nos7, inserting her father's name, fraudulently concocted a story of dissolution between her husband and on the basis of fabricated Amalnama dated 15th Poush, 1350 BS filed the instant case. The Amalnama had never been executed by Surendranath Bandhapadhaya. The Government of the Peoples' Republic of Bangladesh nationalized the entire assets of Dhakeshwari Cotton Mills Limited under President's Order No.27 of 1972. The Management and control over the property had been entrusted upon the Bangladesh Textile Mills Corporation. The appointed Liquidator on behalf of the Government of the Peoples' Republic of Bangladesh made a contract in respect of the entire property of suit plot and other property with Bangladesh Textile Mills Corporation and made over the possession of the property. The Government of the Peoples' Republic of Bangladesh wounded up all the affairs of Dhakeshwari Cotton Mills Limited vide Memo No. MT/A/5-A/83/82-42 dated 25-1-1982. The liquidator on behalf of the Government of the Peoples' Republic of Bangladesh executed and registered deeds of sale in consideration of 7,00,00,000 in 1988. The Defendant No.1 has been in possession of the property. The plaintiff and her husband (i.e. plaintiff No.7) are illegal trespasser- They have no locus standi to file the instant suit and have been trying to delay the legal and lawful process of law. The plaintiff is not entitled to get the relief as prayed for.
5. At the trial both the parties adduced both oral and documentary evidence. The learned Sub-ordinate Judge of Artha Rin Adalat, 3rd Court, Dhaka dismissed the suit on 30-8-1998.
6. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree dated 30-8-1998, the plaintiff filed Title Appeal No.351 of 1998 in the court of District Judge, Dhaka, which was heard by the learned Additional District Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka who after hearing the appeal, allowed the same on 2-5-2000 reversing the judgment and decree 30-8-1998 passed by the trial court.
7. Against the said judgment and decree dated 2-5-2000 the defendant-petitioner filed civil revision No.4687 of 2000 before the High Court Division.
8. A single Bench of the High Court Division after hearing the Rule by the impugned judgment and order dated 22-1-2012 discharged the same.
9. Feeling aggrieved by the said judgment and order, the defendant-petitioner has filed this civil petition for leave to appeal.
10. Mr Md Bodruddoza, learned Advocate, appearing for the petitioner submits that the trial court dismissed the suit on the ground that the plaintiff could not prove the 'Amalnama' by virtue of which she claims title over the suit property and in 1953 Narendra Nath and 5(five) others sold the land in question in favour of Dakeshwari Cotton Mills Ltd. by registered deed, Exhibit F; but neither the lower Appellate Court nor the High Court Division reversed the findings of the trial Court with reference to the evidence as read, as such the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division is liable to be set-aside.
11. The learned Advocate further submits that though the trial Court accepting the gazette notification (Exhibit A) found that the suit land was enlisted as vested property in 1965 and it was vested in the custody of EP1DC and, thereafter, on 2-10-1965 a gazette notification was published and, subsequently, after independence the suit property was vested in favour of BTMC by a gazette notification dated 26-3-1972 (Exhibit B) and in 1982 when Dakeshwari Cotton Mills Ltd., an enterprise of BTMC was put on liquidation by a gazette notification (Exhibit C), the said property was sold by the liquidation sale in favour of BTMC by a registered sale deed dated 21-6-1988 and since then the property is in exclusive control and possession of BTMC, but neither the lower Appellate Court nor the High Court Division considered the title and exclusive possession of BTMC. Hence, the judgment and order of the High Court Division is liable to be set-aside. The learned Advocate lastly submits that in respect of the suit land of Dakeshwari Cotton Mills other persons filed title suit as well as writ petitions and ultimately in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.390 of 2002 this Division has decided that the sale made by the official liquidator of Dakeshwari Cotton Mills Ltd. on 26-6-1988 in favour of BTMC was lawful and though the copy of the judgment of this Division was filed before the High Court Division by way of Supplementary Affidavit as Annexure-"B", the High Court Division overlooked the said judgment and did not mention anything about the judgment of this Division passed in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.390 of 2002 hence, the judgment and order of the High Court Division is liable to be set-aside.
12. Per contra Mr Sharifuddin Chaklader, learned Advocate appearing for the respondents' made submissions in support of the impugned judgment as well as the judgment and decree passed by the court of appeal below.
13. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates for the respective parties, perused the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and other connected papers available on record.
14. In the instant case the plaintiff claims title over the disputed property by virtue of unregistered Amalnama dated 15th of Pous, 1350 BS. The trial Court on proper consideration' of the evidence on record categorically held that the plaintiff failed to prove the said Amalnama, Exhibit 2 and the alleged rent receipts, Exhibits-5 and 5 (Ka) by examining any competent witnesses. However, the court of appeal below believed the said amalnama and decreed the suit holding that the said amalnama and the dakhilas are genuine documents. The Appellate Court in arriving at the above finding did not at all consider the evidence on record and also did not make reference to that effect. An unregistered amalnama without any legal proof ipso facto does not create any right, title, and interest on the suit property in favour of the plaintiff. Further, burden lies heavily upon the plaintiff to prove the unregistered Amalnama when she claims title on the basis of the same, against a registered instrument. In the instant case it reveals from the evidence that the defendant-petitioner has purchased the suit property from liquidator on behalf of the Government by a registered deed being No.1618 dated 21-6-1988, Exhibit F. Previously, the suit property was transferred on 6-10-1953 in favour of the Dhakeshwari. Cotton Mills by the heirs of its original CS record owner. Gopinath Poddar. Eventually, the property was declared as an enemy property by gazette notification dated 6-9-1965, Exhibit A; the management of the property was handed over to erstwhile East Pakistan Industrial Corporation (EPIC) and after independence of Bangladesh pursuant to President's order No.27 of 1972 the said cotton mill along with other properties were nationalized and its Management has been entrusted with the Bangladesh. Textile Mills Corporation (BTMC), Exhibit B and since then BTMC has been possessing and managing the suit property. Eventually, the Liquidation cell made a contract on 11-1-1986 with the present appellant to sell the suit property along with other property, Exhibit .E and thereafter, on 21- 6-1988 liquidation cell executed and registered the sale deed in favour of the BTMC, Exhibit F. SA Khatian was prepared in the name of BTMC.
15. The above facts and documentary evidence have not been considered in its proper and legal perspective by the High Court Division as well as the Court of appeal below and thus, the impugned judgment and order suffers from legal infirmity.
16. It also further emerges from the evidence that the husband of the original plaintiff i.e. present petitioner No.7 was an employee of BTMC, Exhibits-I and G and he was allotted the suit property for residential purpose on payment of rent by BTMC. After his retirement, BTMC on 16-1-1994, 25-44994 and 304-1994 asked him to vacate the property in question by issuing notice.
17. It is also undeniable fact that, when the BTMC asked the petitioner No.7 to vacate the suit property he filed Writ Petition No.390 of 2002 before the High Court Division and eventually, the Rule Nisi was discharged for default. The petitioner No.7 filed an application before the. High Court Division to restore the said writ petition. However, the said application was also rejected on merit; against which petitioner No.7 preferred Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.390 of 2002 before this Division. This Division after hearing the leave petition dismissed the same holding to the effect that:
"It appears that the petitioners have no right, title and interest in the case properties concerned. It may be that they are licensees and/or leases but they have no legal title to the case properties to resist the sale made by the official liquidator of Dhakeswari Cotton Mills Ltd. in favour of BTMC. The petitioners have no locus-standi to challenge the action of the respondents. Therefore, submissions made by the learned Advocate for the petitioner merit no consideration."
18. Prior to filing the writ petition, the petitioner No.7 as plaintiff filed Title Suit No.25 of 1995 in connection with the suit property in the court of Sub- ordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka for a declaration that he is a legal possessor in the suit property and having failed to get ad-interim order of injunction he along with others filed Title Suit No.146 of 1995 in the same Court for a declaration that they are entitled to get allotment of the suit property from the Government. The petitioner No.7 also filed Rent Suit No.57 of 1973 before the Sub-ordinate Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka impleading the BTMC.
19. When the petitioner No.7 failed to establish his title in the suit property by filing civil suits and writ petition, then his wife as plaintiff came forward to establish her title on the basis of an unregistered amalnama and also with a plea that her husband divorced her. Exhibit K, proves that petitioner No.7 appointed her as his 'Nominee' in order to get pension benefit. Further, the plaintiff at no point of time has challenged Exhibit A, gazette notification enlisting the suit property as enemy property and, Exhibit B, the order of nationalization of the suit property pursuant to President's Order No.27 of 1972.
20. Article 10 and 10(1A) of the President's Order No.27 of 1972 [The Bangladesh Industrial
Enterprises (Nationalisation) Order, 1972] runs as follows:
10.(1) On the commencement of this Order, there shall be established the following corporations:
"(a)………………………
(b) [Bangladesh Textile Mills Corporation], which shall have and exercise all the powers of a corporation in respect of all the industrial enterprises engaged in cotton manufacturing enumerated in the Second Schedule;
(c)…………………………….
(d) ………………………………
"(1A) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law, an industrial enterprise, placed under any Corporation by an order notified in the official Gazette under sub-clause (d) of clause (1) of Article 10, and all shares or other proprietary interest in such industrial enterprise shall be deemed to have always vested in the Government and no such order shall be challenged on the ground that the industrial enterprise or the shares or interest therein had not vested in the  Government, or that the industrial  enterprise, or any share or interest therein,  was not liable to be vested in the Government."
<u>21. In view of the above provisions of law, there is no scope to challenge the order of nationalization, notified in the gazette by the Government and thus, suit is not maintainable.</u>
22. Having considered and discussed as above, we find merit in the leave petition; however we are not inclined to grant leave, since we have heard the parties at length.
23. Accordingly, the leave petition is disposed of.
Judgment and order dated 22-1-2012 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.4687 of 2000 affirming the judgment and decree dated 2-5-2000 passed by the Additional District Judge, 5th Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No.351 of 1998 is hereby set-aside. Judgment and decree passed by the Trial Court in Title Suit No.101 of 1997 passed by the Artha Rin Adalat, 3rd Court and Sub-ordinate Judge, Dhaka is restored.
End.

case_source: (From the judgment and decree dated 2-2-2017 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.946 of 2000)
full_judgment:
Hasan Foez Siddique, CJ: This appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 2-2-2017 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.946 of 2000 reversing the judgment and decree dated 2-2-1999 passed by the learned Joint District Judge Artha Rin Adalat, Faridpur in Title Appeal No.243 of 1992 reversing those dated 7-9-1992 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Alfadanga, Faridpur in Title Suit No.62 of 1985.
2. The relevant facts, for the disposal of this appeal, are that Shafiuddin and another instituted aforesaid suit for declaration of their title and recovery of khas possession stating that the land as described in the schedule to the plaint belonged to Maizuddin who died leaving behind one son, Plaintiff No.1 and widow the plaintiff No.2 as his heirs. The plaintiffs, constructing dwelling homestead in 0.17 acre of land of plot No.187, had been residing therein. The defendants forcibly dispossessed the plaintiffs on 25-10-1985. The plaintiffs came to know that SA record of right in respect of the suit land was wrongly prepared in the names of the defendants. Hence, was the suit.
3. The defendant No.1 contested the suit contending that the landlords of the disputed joma were Nagendra Roy Mukhopadhya and others and tenant was Maizuddin. Maizuddin defaulted to pay the rent. Thus, the landlords, instituting a Rent Suit, got decree and took over the said property in his possession executing the said decree. Thereafter, Baser Mollah, predecessor-in-interest of the defendant, took settlement of the said land from the landlords and took over possession of the same. SA record was prepared in the name of the plaintiff No.1. Accordingly, the defendant filed objection case which was allowed. This defendant has been possessing the suit land for more than 12 years. The suit should be dismissed.
4. The trial Court, on consideration of the evidence on record, dismissed the suit. The plaintiffs preferred appeal, which was allowed by the appellate Court.
5. Then the defendant filed civil revisional application in the High Court Division and obtained Rule. The High Court Division by the impugned judgment and order made the said Rule absolute. Against the aforesaid judgment and order of the High Court division, appellants have preferred this appeal upon getting leave.
6. Mr Md Nurul Amin, learned Senior Counsel appearing for the appellants, submits that the plaintiffs are the successive heirs of CS recorded tenants and they were in possession of the suit land till the date of dispossession on 25-10-1985 and the plaintiffs, by adducing sufficient evidences, proved their title and possession and, thereafter, date of dispossession. He submits that the last Court of facts upon proper appreciation of the evidence on record, found plaintiffs' title, possession and their dispossession in the suit land, the High court Division erred in law in setting aside the well reasoned judgment of the appellate Court. He further submits that the defendants claimed that the suit land was sold in auction and the landlords auction purchased the same and took over the possession of the same, thereafter settled the suit land to the predecessor-in-interest of the contesting defendants but they hopelessly failed to prove the story of alleged auction and their allegedly settlement, the High Court Division upon improper consideration of the evidence adduced by the parties erroneously dismissed the suit.
7. Mr Garib Newaz, learned Advocate appearing for the respondents, submits that it is the duty of the plaintiffs to prove their own case to get the decree and their possession in the suit land till the date of dispossession, the High Court Division upon proper appreciation of the materials on record, rightly reversed the judgment and decree of the appellate Court. He further submits since the plaintiffs failed to prove their possession till the date of their dispossession, the trial Court as well as the revisional Court upon proper appreciation of the evidence on record, came to the conclusion that the plaintiffs suit was barred by limitation.
8. Admittedly, Moizuddin was CS recorded tenant. The plaintiffs' case is that they are the successive heirs of the said Moizuddin and had been possessing the suit land till the date of their dispossession dated 25-10-1985. At the initial stage, SA record-of-rights was prepared in their names but finally it was published in the name of contesting defendants. It was their case that the plaintiff No.1 who is PW 1 was minor at the time of preparation of record-of-rights and the contesting defendant was his close relative and after the death of his father, they started to live in the house of the defendants. Taking opportunity of his minority, the defendant forcedly dispossessed the plaintiff from the suit land.
9. It appears from the materials on record that earlier before the publication of SA operation, a Miscellaneous Case for correction of record-of-rights was filed which was disposed of on contest. Finally SA record-of-rights was prepared and published in the name of defendant No.1. On perusal of the judgment of the trial Court it appears that the Trial Court considered the oral and documentary evidence adduced by the parties and came to the conclusion that the plaintiffs have failed to prove their possession till their alleged date of dispossession from the suit land. It further held that the suit was barred by limitation. While drawing conclusion as to the possession of the plaintiffs till their dispossession, the first Court of fact considered the evidence adduced by the parties vividly but from the judgment and decree of the appellate Court it appears that the appellate Court, without taking into consideration of the evidence as quoted by the trial Court, abruptly reversed the finding as to the possession of the plaintiffs till their dispossession from the suit land. The revisional Court reversed the finding as to the possession and dispossession arrived at the appellate Court holding that the conclusion arrived at by the last Court of fact is not based on evidence. In the plaint, the plaintiffs stated that they were dispossessed by the defendant on 25-10-1985 from the suit land, plaintiff No.1 was examined as PW 1 who in his evidence did not utter a word about the alleged date of dispossession. Similarly their another witness PW 2 has also said nothing about the date of dispossession of the plaintiffs from the same. We have also gone through the judgment of the Courts below it appears to us that the conclusion arrived at by the High Court Division is correct.
<u>10. The appellate Court mainly relied upon the weakness of the case of the defendants that they have failed to prove of the story auction sale and their alleged settlement but in order to get a decree for recovery of possession along with prayer for declaration of title the weakness of the defendants case cannot be a ground for getting decree the plaintiffs, particularly, when the plaintiffs failed to prove their possession in the suit land till their dispossession.</u>
11. In such view of the matter, we do not find any substance in the instant appeal.
Thus, the appeal is dismissed.
End.
