full_judgment:
Md Faruque (M. Faruque), J: Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the Memo No. 49.008.011.0977. 00.2075.2010-330 dated 8-7-2013 (Annexure-L) issued by the respondent No. 3 cancelling the petitioner's license being No. RL-977 and thereby forfeiting the entire security deposits against the said recruiting license of the petitioner under section 14 of the Emigration Ordinance, 1982 and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.
2. At the time of issuance of the Rule the operation of the impugned Memo No. 49.008. 011.0977.00.2075.2010-330 dated 8-7-2013 (Annexure-L) was stayed.
3. The short facts, for disposal of the Rule are that the petitioner is a private limited company being registered with the Register of Joint Stock Company and engaged in manpower business having recruiting agency and the petitioner is the member of Bangladesh Association of International Recruiting Agencies (BAIRA). The petitioner has been granted a recruiting license being No.RL-977 by observing all the formalities under Section 10 of the Emigration Ordinance, 1982 to conduct the business of a recruiting agency.
4. The respondent No. 2 issued a notice vide Memo No. ESRL-2285/2005/2011 dated 27-9-2012 (Annexure-D) upon the petitioner stating that the Ministry of Manpower, Singapore did not authorize First Care Employment Agency in relation to the appointment of 5,000 Bangladeshi Workers and Bangladesh High Commission did not attest any demand letter in favour of the petitioner and accordingly asked the petitioner to give a reply from the within 7(seven) days.
5. The petitioner on 7-10-2013 sent a reply to the respondent No. 2 in relation to the show cause notice dated 27-9-2012 stating that the petitioner had no knowledge about the allegation of the show cause notice and the petitioner did not send any worker to the said company of Singapore and the petitioner did not give any power of authority and also did not take any money in the name of that company of Singapore. (Annexure-E).
6. The Director, Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Trading formed an investigation team for investigation to submit a report about the demand letter for 5,000 Bangladeshi Workers to the First Care Employment Agency by forgoing seal and signature of First Secretary (Labour), Singapore, Bangladesh High Commission and also requested the investigation team to submit a report within 10(ten) working days vide Memo No. ESRL 2285/2005 dated 26-11-2012. The Deputy Director and Investigation Officer, Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Trading issued a letter vide Memo No. ESRL-977/z/2012 /2437 dated 29-11-2012 before the investigation officer in person with a written statement and related evidence to the said allegation. (Annexure-F).
7. Thereafter, respondent No. 3 issued a show cause notice vide memo No. 49.008.011. 0833.00.101.2010-11 dated 10-1-2013 upon the petitioner as to why the license of the petitioner shall not be cancelled and the securities of the petitioner shall not be forfeited according to section 14 of the Emigration Ordinance, 1982 and also asked the petitioner submit to reply of that show cause notice within 15 (Fifteen) days. (Annexure-H)
8. Thereafter, the petitioner sent a reply to the Secretary, Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employer Affairs in relation to the show cause notices dated 10-1-2013 stating that the petitioner had no knowledge about the said allegation and moreso the Investigation Team did not find any connection of the petitioner with the said allegation and accordingly prayed for discharging him from the said allegation. (Annexure-I).
9. The respondent No. 3 again issued another show cause notice vide Memo No. 49. 008.011.0033.00.101.2010-179 dated 2-4-2013 upon the petitioner stating that the petitioner failed to submit any documentary evidence in relation to one namely Md Hossain and accordingly the liability of making forged seal and signature goes to the petitioner and hence the respondent No. 3 according to section 104 of the Emigration Ordinance, 1982 asked the petitioner as to why the license of the petitioner shall not be cancelled and the securities of the petitioner shall not be forfeited and also requested the petitioner to submit a reply within 15 (Fifteen) days. (Annexure-J).
10. The petitioner submitted a reply to the Secretary, Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employer Affairs in relation to the show cause notice dated 2-4-2013 stating that the investigation team did not find any connection of the petitioner with the said allegation and moreso gave the address and telephone number of Md Hossain mentioning that the petitioner is willing to give testimony at any time and prayed for discharging him from the said allegation. (Annexure-K).
11. Thereafter, the respondent No. 3 cancelled the license of the petitioner and forfeited the securities of the petitioner under section 14 of the Emigration Ordinance, 1982 vide Memo No. 49.008.011.0977.00.2075.2010-330 dated 8-7-2013 stating that the petitioner failed to submit any evidence in relation to confirmation of Md Hossen with the allegation (Annexure-L). The petitioner having no other alternative and efficacious remedy, filed this writ petitioner under Article 102 of the Constitution of People's Republic of Bangladesh and obtained the instant Rule.
12. The learned Advocate Mr Mizanul Hogue Chowdhury appearing for the petitioner submits that section 14 of the Emigration Ordinance, 1982 provides that Government may cancel license after making inquiry and by giving opportunity of being heard to the licensee but in the instant case the respondents issued as many as 4 (four) show cause notices upon the petitioner and accordingly the petitioner replied the said show cause notices and also expressed his desire to participate in the hearing vide reply dated 27-4-2013 but the respondents without giving any opportunity to the petitioner issued the impugned order cancelling the license of the petitioner and forfeiting the securities which is violative of section 14 of the Emigration Ordinance, 1982. In this context the learned Advocate referred the case of Government of Bangladesh and others vs Tajul Islam reported in 4 MLR (AD) 5 = 4 BLC (AD) 160.
13. He further submits that the respondents did not supply the inquiry report along with the show cause notice before cancelling the license and forfeiting the securities which is violative of section 14 of the Emigration Ordinance, 1982 and also violation of principle of natural justice and the impugned order' has been passed at the direction of the Bangladesh High Commission, Singapore. Therefore the respondent No. 3 failed to exercise his own discretion considering the reply of the petitioner which is evident from the impugned order as such the impugned order is liable to be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.
14. He submits that the petitioner cannot run his business due to cancellation of the licensee and he has been deprived from his right to life, livelihood, business as guaranteed under Articles 31, 32 and 40 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh.
15. Rule has been contested by the respondent No. 2 by filing affidavit-in-opposition wherein it has been stated that the petitioner was given opportunity of being heard appearing before the respondent No. 3. The investigation team mentioned in the investigation report that Md Hossain is a Bangladeshi national, worked as a representative of the petitioner who managed the demand letters for sending workers abroad by the petitioner. But while the address of Md Hossain was asked by the investigating team, the petitioner failed to give the address of Md Hossain which proved the involvement of the petitioner with the allegation.
16. By filing another supplementary affidavit dated 8-8-2018 for the respondent No. 2 the learned Advocate Mr Tanvir Parvez submits that the Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employment came to learn about the forged demand note from a letter dated 27-7-2012 issued by the First Secretary (Labour) of the Bangladesh High Commission in Singapore. The respondent No. 2 cannot confirm as to whether the copy of the inquiry report was given to the writ petitioner and the record does not show anything that the copy was given to the writ-petitioner. He also submits that the petitioner is not entitled to get a copy of the inquiry report, as such the petitioner's right under the principle of natural justice had not been breached. The Ministry of Expatriate Welfare and Overseas Employment has not initiated any action against Md Hossain.
17. We have heard the learned Advocate for the writ-petitioner and the learned Advocate for the respondent No. 2, perused the impugned letter, writ petition and other materials on record.
18. It appears that the petitioner is a private limited company duly registered in the Register of Joint Stock Company and engaged in manpower business having recruiting agency and the petitioner is a member of Bangladesh Association of International Recruiting Agencies (BAIRA). The petitioner has been granted a recruiting license being No.RL-977 under Section 10 of the Emigration Ordinance, 1982 to conduct the business of a recruiting agency. The respondent No. 2 issued a notice vide Memo No. ESRL-2285/2005/2011 dated 27-9-2012 upon the petitioner stating that the Ministry of Manpower, Singapore did not authorize First Care Employment Agency in relation to the appointment of 5000 Bangladeshi Workers and Bangladesh High Commission did not attest any demand letter in favor of the petitioner and accordingly asked for a reply from the petitioner within 7(seven) days. On 7-10-2013 the petitioner sent a reply to the respondent No. 2 in relation to the show cause notice dated 27-9-2012 stating that the petitioner had no knowledge about the allegation of the show cause notice stating that the petitioner company did not send any worker to the said company of Singapore. The petitioner-company also stated that the company did not give any power of authority to any person and has not take any money in the name of that company of Singapore.
19. The Director, Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Trading formed an investigation team for investigation and to submit a report about the demand letter for 5000 Bangladeshi Workers to the First Care Employment Agency by forgoing seal and signature of First Secretary (Labour), Singapore, High Commission and the investigation team asked to submit a report within 10(ten) working days vide Memo No. ESRL 2285/2005 dated 26-11-2012. The Deputy Director and Investigation Officer, Bureau of Manpower, Employment and Trading issued a letter vide Memo No. ESRL-977/z414/2012/ 2437 dated 29-11-2012 before the investigation officer in person with a written statement and related evidence to the said allegation. Thereafter, the respondent No. 3 issued a show cause notice vide memo No. 49.008.011.0833.00. 101.2010-11 dated 10-1-2013 upon the petitioner as to why the license of the petitioner shall not be cancelled and the securities of the petitioner shall not be forfeited according to section 14 of the Emigration Ordinance, 1982 and also requested the petitioner to submit a reply of that show cause notice within 15 (Fifteen) days.
20. It appears from the record that the petitioner sent a reply to the Secretary, Ministry of Expatriates' Welfare and Overseas Employer Affairs in relation to the show cause notices dated 10-1-2013 stating that the petitioner had no knowledge about the said allegation. Thereafter, the Investigation Team did not find any connection of the petitioner with the said allegation and accordingly prayed for discharging him from the said allegation.
21. The respondent No. 3 again issued another show cause notice vide Memo No. 49.008.011.0033.00.101.2010-179 dated 2-4-2013 upon the petitioner stating that the petitioner failed to submit any documentary evidence in relation to one namely Md Hossain and accordingly the liability of making forged seal and signature goes to the petitioner and hence the Respondent No. 3 according to section 104 of the Emigration Ordinance, 1982 asked the petitioner as to why the license of the petitioner shall not be cancelled and the securities of the petitioner shall not be forfeited and also requested the petitioner to submit a reply within 15 (Fifteen) days. Thereafter, the petitioner submitted a reply to the Secretary, Ministry of Expatriate Welfare and Overseas Employer Affairs in relation to the show cause notice dated 2-4-2013 stating that the investigation team did not find any connection of the petitioner with the said allegation and the petitioner has no relation with the said Md Hossain or any other person to the First Secretary, Singapore and the petitioner never submitted the demand letter for 5,000 person or any person to the concerned Ministry and the alleged Mohamad Hossain is not connected with the petitioner company. The petitioner also stated that he is willing to give testimony at any time and prayed for discharging him from the said allegation. But the respondent No. 3 cancelled the license of the petitioner and forfeited the securities of the petitioner under section 14 of the Emigration Ordinance, 1982 vide Memo No. 49.008.011.0977.00.2075.2010-330 dated 8-7-2013 which cannot be sustainable in the eye of law.
22. Section 14 of the Emigration Ordinance, 1982 clearly provides that before cancelling the licensee, an opportunity of being heard must be given to the petitioner. The said section is reproduced below:
Section 14(1)—"If, at any time during the pendency of a license, the Government is satisfied, after making such enquiry as it may deem necessary, that the licensee has been guilty of misconduct or that his conduct or performance as a licensee has been unsatisfactory or that he has violated any of the provisions of the Ordinance or the rules made thereunder or the prescribed Code of Conduct, it may, after giving the licensee an opportunity of being heard, by order in writing, cancel the licence or suspend it for a period to be specified in the order and may also forfeit the security furnished by him under section 10 in full or part."
23. In the case of Government of Bangladesh and others vs Tnjul Islam reported in 4 MLR (AD) 5 = 4 BLC (AD) 160 their Lordships held that:
"Section 14(1)—Cancellation of license without proper show cause notice—Violative of natural justice—Government have the power to suspend or cancel licence under section 14 of the Ordinance on the ground of misconduct and violations of the relevant provisions of the Ordinance. But in doing so the licensee must be given sufficient notice to show cause and reasonable opportunity of being heard. Licence is a legal privilege granted under law and not a charity. The show cause notice is not a mere technicality or idle ceremony. The notice must be clear and contain the facts of allegations. When the notice is vague it is no notice in the eye of law. Cancellation of licence without proper notice to show cause and without opportunity of representing the defence being arbitrary and violative of the principle of natural justice is not sustainable in law."
24. Section 14 of the Immigration Ordinance, 1982 and the settled principle of law derives from the decision of our Apex Court stated above, it is a mandatory provision of law that before cancellation of a license, the authority must give a chance to the licensee of being heard, failing which the cancellation has no basis in the eye of law.
25. In this case, the order does not show nor there is anything on record to show that the respondent has given any chance of hearing to the petitioner before making such an order of cancellation and forfeiture of securities. Therefore, the order is violative of the section 14(1) of the ordinance and was thus bad in law. We shall confine to the allegation of not giving the petitioner an opportunity of being heard before issuing the impugned order dated 8-3-2013 (Annexure-L), we find that there was no hearing at all.
<u>26. A license in a commercial sense is not a charity done to a person but a privilege accorded generally on payment of fee. So, the cancellation of a license is a serious matter, adversely touching a, person's pecuniary interest. More than that, it affects a fundamental right of a citizen to conduct any lawful trade or business subject to certain restrictions imposed by law. The Court would always insist that an authority exercising such a drastic power of cancellation, do act strictly according to law and always with fairness. The writ Court will not examine and weigh the aggrieved person's case on merit as an Appellate Court but to ensure that he was given a fair deal by the authority in accordance with law.</u>
27. In the instant case, the order of cancellation of the license and forfeiture of securities of the petitioner even does not show that the Government was either "satisfied" as required under section 14(1) or that the petitioner's long representation was ever brought to its notice. The impugned order thus was a bad order in the eye of law.
28. In view of the above facts and circumstance of the case, we find that the impugned order issued by the respondent No. 3 cancelling the petitioner's recruiting license being No. RL-977 and forfeiting the entire securities, deposited by the petitioner (Annexure-L) was not in accordance with law.
29. In the result, the Rule is made absolute.
30. Impugned memo No. 49.008.011.0977. 00.2075.2010-330 dated 8-7-2013 (Annexure-L) issued by the respondent No. 3 cancelling the petitioner's license being No. RL-977 and forfeiting the entire security deposits against the said recruiting license of the petitioner under section 14 of the Emigration Ordinance, 1982 is declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.
31. The respondents are directed to renew the license of the petitioner subject to payment of all arrears of renewal fees in accordance with law within 3(three) months from the date of receipt of this judgment and order.
However, there shall be no order as to cost.
End.

lawyer:
Uzzal Bhowmick with Tonay Kumar Saha, Advocates —For the Appellants
Probir Neogi Senior Advocate with Subrata Saha, Tapos Bandhu Das and Sanehadri Chakrabarty, Advocates —For the Respondents
parties:
Anil Chandra Sarker and others………………Appellants
Vs
Joydeb Chandra Mondal and others…………Respondents
full_judgment:
Bhishmadev Chakrabortty, J: Defendants 1-5 have preferred this appeal against the judgment and decree of the Joint District Judge, Court No.2, Gazipur passed on 25-7-2019 in Title Suit No.26 of 2011 decreeing the suit for partition.
2. The plaint case, in brief, is that Din Mondal alias Dinu Mondal was the owner of the schedule suit land. Dinu Mondal died leaving behind his wife Dukhi Bewa and 2(two) daughters Sahachari and Gayahwari. According to Dayabhaga System of Hindu Law Dinu's wife Dukhi Bewa got life estate in the suit land left by him. Dukhi Bewa had no son and as such her elder daughter Sahachari was given in marriage with one Shreecharan Mondal and he was kept in her house as domesticated son-in-law. The suit land was recorded in CS khatian 177 in the name of Dukhi Bewa and Shreecharan Mondal to the extent of 8 annas share each but Shreecharan Mondal had no title over the suit land. During her possession and enjoyment Dukhi Bewa sold 0.37 acres from plot 70 to Surendar Chandra Sarker and others for the legal necessity and handed over possession thereof. Accordingly, the said 0.37 acres of land was recorded in SA khatian 346 and RS khatian 49 in the name of Surendra Chandra and others. Subsequently, Dukhi Bewa died leaving behind her 2(two) daughters Sahachari and Gayahwari Mondal. As per Dayabhaga system they got life interest in the land left by Dukhi Bewa except the land measuring 0.37 acres texhibitransferred by Dukhi. Gayashwari subsequently died leaving behind his only son Ashwani Kumar Mondal the father of defendants 1-3 and grandfather of defendants 4 and 5 and her sister Sahachari Mondal. In this way Sahachari Mondal acquired life interest over the property left by Dukhi Bewa measuring an area of 5.25 acres. Sahachari died leaving behind his 3(three) sons Kiron Mondal, Dinesh Mondal and Haripada Mondal and thus Ashwani, Kiron, Dinesh and Haripada Mondal acquired the suit land as grandson of Dinu Mondal in equal shares i.e., each of them got ¼ th of property measuring an area of 1.3125 acres. In SA operation SA khatian 345 in respect of 5.25 acres was recorded in the name of Gayasshari's husband Ananda Mondal and Sahachari's husband Shreecharan Mondal along with titleless Madhab Mondal and Profulla Kumar Mondal. In RS operation, RS khatian 15 measuring an area of 5.31 acres (0.06 acres land) was recorded 8 annas in the name of Gayasshari's son Ashwani Kumar and remaining 8 annas in the name of Kiron, Dinesh and Haripada, the sons of Sahachari. During their possession and enjoyment Ashwani Mondal transferred 0.65 acres to Kiron, Dinesh and Haripada by a registered kabala dated 1-11-1969 from RS Khatian 15 corresponding to SA khatian 345 and handed over possession thereof. Kiron, Dinesh and Horipada got 3.9375 acres by inheritance and also 0.6150 acres by purchase measuring total 4.5525 acres from SA khatian 345 corresponding to RS khatian 15. They sold 0.04 acres to defendants 20 and 21 and remained in possession in 4.5525 acres. During their possession and enjoyment Kiron Chandra died leaving behind his 2(two) sons Parimal and Nirmal plaintiffs 5 and 6; Dinesh, Haripada, Parimal and Nirmol during their possession and enjoyment over 4.5125 acres sold 0.63 acres to defendant 24 and remained in possession over 3.8825 acres. Haripada died leaving behind his 4(four) sons Maran Chandra Sarker, Bimal Chandra Sarker, Kamal Chandra Sarker and Sujan Chandra Sarker. In this way the plaintiffs have been owning and possessing 3.8825 acres by erecting houses thereon and planting trees. In 2004, the son of Gayahwari mutated his name in respect of the suit land showing his share to the extent 8 annas then it came to the knowledge of the plaintiffs and they filed an objection against the said mutation and it was cancelled in 2013. The defendants refused to partition the land showing the shares of the plaintiffs to the extent ¾ share of the total land then they instituted the suit praying for shaham over the land as detailed to the schedule of the plaint.
3. The defendants 1-5 contested the suit by filing written statement denying the statement made in the plaint. They contended that the suit is not maintainable in the present form and manner and it is barred by limitation. They further contended that Dukhi. Bewa was the owner of land measuring 5.62 acres. Dukhi Bewa had 2(two) daughters Sahachari and Gayashwari. The husband of Shahachari namely Shreecharan Mondal was kept in her house as domesticated son-in-law. CS khatian 177 was prepared wrongly showing 8 annas share to Dukhi and Sreecharan each but actually Dukhi Bewa was the owner of the total land. The defendant after examination of witnesses on 1-8-2018 amended the written statement and incorporated the fact that the suit property was owned by Dukhi Bewa as Yatuka at the time of her marriage and consequently it will be treated as her Stridhana. They admitted that Dukhi Bewa sold 0.37 acres of plot 70 to Surendra Chandra Sarker and others and during her possession and enjoyment on remaining land measuring 5.25 acres she gave her daughter Gayahwari to marriage with Ananda Mondal and kept him in her house as domesticated son-in-law. In 1940 she partitioned the land between his 2(two) daughters and each of the daughters got 2.625 acres. During possession and enjoyment through the husbands of 2(two) daughters SA record in respect of 5.25 acres was recorded in the name of Shreecharan and Ananda and erroneously the names of Madab Mondal and Profullo Mondal were included in the khatian but they have no title and possession over the suit land. Sahachari Mondal died leaving behind his 3(three) sons Kiron Chandra, Dinesh Chandra and Haripada and they inherited the property left by Sahachari in equal shares. Gayahwari died leaving behind her only son Ashwani Kumar Mandal and he inherited 8 annas share enjoyed by her mother. Ashwani during his possession and enjoyment transferred 0.28 acres to Minor Hossain, 0.15 acres to Montu Shah, 0.13 acres to Chondi Dash, Nipendranath and Raton Mondal and .24 acres to Md Rohman and others. Apart from the above transfer, he transferred 0.615 acres to the 3(three) sons of Sahachari Mondal i.e., the predecessors of the plaintiffs. Aashwani Kumar Mondal further sold 0.04 acres to defendant 3 and 0.285 acres to defendant 24. Thus he totally transferred 1.74 acres from the suit property and had been enjoying and possession of the remaining part. He mutated his name in the year 2004 to the extent of 8 annas share of the suit jote and died leaving behind the defendants 1-5 as heirs. The father of the plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No.132 of 2003 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Court No.4, Gazipur which was dismissed on 27-10-2005. The plaintiffs have no title and possession over the land measuring an area of 0.885 acres having been enjoyed by the defendants. The suit has been filed on false averments and as such it would be dismissed.
4. The trial Court on pleadings framed as many as 5 issues to adjudicate the matter in dispute. Amongst other the issue whether the plaintiff is entitled to get a decree for partition as prayed for. During trial, the plaintiff examined 4 witnesses and Exhibited their documents Exhibits 1-4 series, while the defendants examined 4 witnesses and their documents were Exhibited as Exhibits Ka-Cha. However, the trial Court considering the evidence and other materials on record by the judgment and decree under challenge decreed the suit on the finding that the plaintiffs have been able to prove that Dukhi Bewa enjoyed and possessed the suit land as life estate. The defendant failed to prove that the property was obtained by Dukhi Bewa as Stridhana.
5. Mr Uzzal Bhowmick, learned Advocate for the appellants takes us through the materials on record and submits that the plaintiff although claimed that Dinu Mondal was the original owner of the suit land but they failed to lead any positive evidence supporting the contention. Admittedly CS record was prepared in the name of Dukhi Bewa showing his share to the extent of 8 annas. The presumption of preparation of CS record is to be rebuted by the plaintiff through evidence. Subsequently, 2(two) records were prepared in conformity of the CS record. In SA record the names of the husbands of 2(two) daughters of Dukhi Bewa were recorded with the name of some other title less persons and RS record was prepared in the name of Ashwini Kumar Mondal to the extent of 8 annas share which supports that Dukhi Bewa obtained the suit land as Yatuka and it was her stridhana. Although, the said claim of the defendants about Stridhana was incorporated by amended of the written statement at a belated stage but it was nothing but a better statement. The defendants proved their case by Exhibiting CS, SA and RS khatian Exhibits-Ka-Gha. He refers to the deed of purchase of the plaintiffs predecessor Exhibit-5 and submits that through the said documents the plaintiff processor purchased land from 3 plots to the extent of 8 arenas share of each plot. The plaintiffs thus admitted the title of 8 annas share of the defendant Ashwani over the suit land. While the sons of Sahachari admitted the title of the defendant to the extent of 8 annas share, their sons cannot undo those after expiry of long years. He refers to the statement of paragraph-Cha of the written statement and submits that Dukhi Bewa in the year 1940 partitioned of the suit land between his 2(two) daughters which has been admitted by PW2 and supported by the evidence of DW 4. The plaintiff did not deny it by cross-examining DW 4. The title and possession over the suit land has been admitted by the first generation, second generation and third generation, now the plaintiffs being fourth generation cannot disown it. The subsequent 2 records, i.e., SA and RS support the aforesaid partition by Dukhi Bewa. It is admitted position of fact that Ashwani Kumar being the son of Gayashwari transferred more than 4 annas share of the suit land. The plaintiffs' present suit without challenging those documents and claiming title over the suit land and without making any prayer for correction of the record of rights is not maintainable. The facts and circumstances and the transfer by Ashwani Kumar proves that he got the suit land per stripes. The trial Court without entering into the facts and evidence on record erred in law and thereby decreed the suit which is to be interfered with by this Court in this appeal.
6. Mr Probir Neogi, learned Senior Advocate appearing for the respondents submits that the defendants totally failed to prove that the property in question was Stridhana of Dukhi Bewa. Their claim to get 8 annas of Dukhi Bewa's property by Ashwani son Gayashwari fails paving the way to success of the partition suit as claimed by the plaintiffs. He submits that in the original written statement the story of Stridhana was not stated but it was incorporated on 1-8-2018 after 7 years of the institution of the suit, i.e. after conclusion of the examination of the plaintiffs' witnesses. It clearly shows that this sort of amendment was afterthought and concocted. He refers to the provision of section 105 of the Code of Civil Procedure and submits that the plaintiff although did not challenge it to the higher Court at that time that and it was merged with the judgment but at this stage they can raise the port of allowing such sort of amendment. The trial Court also found that although the defendants predecessor Ashwani transferred his major share from the suit jote but suppressing those facts he mutated his name in the concerned office showing his share to the extent of 8 annas. He then submits that although in the written statement, the defendants contended that Dukhi Bewa gave the property to her two daughters in equal share whereby the property was partitioned by Dukhi Bewa herself during her lifetime but it has been consistently held by our Apex Court that mutual family arrangement for convenience of enjoyment of the property does not amount to partition. Moreover, since both Sahachari and Gayashwari owned and possessed the property as life estate but after death of both of them the property went to the legal heirs of original owner Dinu Mondal and they are Dinu Mondal's daughters' sons. The property admittedly stands recorded in RS khatian No.15 in the name of both parties. Although showing the shares wrongly in the name of Ashwani to the extent of 8 annas. This contention of the defendants is legally infirm and rightly rejected by the trial Court. He refers to the case of Probir Kumar Rakshit vs Abdus Sabur, 14 BLC (AD) 28; Rajendranath Saha @ Rajendra Pradan Saha and another vs Md Sonaullah Pramanik and others, 42 DLR 393 and Abdul Noor Q Cunnu Miah and another vs Makhan Miah Q Md Laisuzzaman and others, 12 MLR (AD) 347 and relied on the ratio laid therein. Mr Neogi then submits that earlier the plaintiff instituted Title Suit No.132 of 2003 which was dismissed for default on 27-1-2005 and the cause of action for a partition suit being recurrent which exists till the property is partitioned by metes and bounds, the present partition suit is therefore squarely competent and maintainable. In the aforesaid premises the trial Court correctly decreed the suit which may not be interfered with by this Court.
7. We have considered the submissions of both the sides and gone through the materials on record, particularly the plaint, written statement, the oral evidence lead by the parties and the documents submitted. It is admitted that Dukhi Bewa was the wife of Dinu Mondal. It is also admitted position of fact that CS record was prepared in the name of Dukhi Bewa and Shreecharan Mondal to the extent of 8 annas share each. It is further admitted that SA record was prepared in the name of Shreecharan and Ananda Mondal along with the name of some other titleless persons. It is also admitted that Dukhi Bewa died leaving behind his 2(two) daughters Sahachari and Gayashwari and it is further admitted that Sahachari died leaving behind her 3(three) sons Kiran, Dinesh and Haripada and Gayashwari leaving behind his only son Ashwani Kumar. The claim of plaintiff-respondent is that Dinu Mondal was the original owner of the suit land measuring an area of 5.62 as detailed to the schedule of the plaint. After his death Dukhi Bewa got life estate over the suit land. On the other hand, the defendants claim that Dukhi Bewa obtained the suit land as Yatuka from her father and she partitioned the land between 2(two) daughter Sahachari and Gayashwari in the 1940. The defendants did not disown that Dinu Mondal was the husband of Dukhi Bewa. It appears that if the fact of partition of the land by Dukhi Bewa in the year 1940 it taken as true the SA record published in the year 1963 finally would have been prepared in the name Sahachari and Gayashwari but it was prepared in the name of Shreecharan and Ananda along with other titleless persons. It proves that Dukhi Bewa got the suit property as life estate on the death of her husband Dinu Mondal and since she had no son her two domesticated son-in-law Shreecharan and Ananda enjoyed the suit land on behalf of them as they acquired life estate in the suit land. The fact of obtaining the suit land by Dukhi Bewa was incorporated in the written statement after conclusion of the examination of plaintiffs' witnesses. On scrutinizing the record we do not find that any evidence was led supporting the claim of the defendants of Yatuka. The fact of obtaining the suit land as Yatuka from the father of Dukhi Bewa is also proved false by the evidence of DW1. In evidence PW1 he stated that “বিয়ের পর দুখি বেওয়া সুত্রাপুর আসে সত্য”. It mines that after the marriage Dukhi Bewa came to the place, where her husband resided and the suit property situated. Therefore, the suit land cannot be Yatuka property of Dukhi Bews.
<u>8. It has come from the evidence of both the sides that the suit property was never partitioned by metes and bounds and both the parties possess the suit land in ejmali. It is well settled position of law that amicable arrangement for separate possession of joint land among the co-sharers itself does not amount to partition or exclusive possession put an end to legal title of other co-shares by adverse possession. In the case of Md Abdul Noor alias Chunnu Mia and another vs Makhan Mia alias Md Laisuzzaman and others, 12 MLR (AD) 347 as referred to by Mr Neogi it has been held:</u>
<u>"It is needless to mention here that an amicable partition is no partition in the eye of law. A co-sharer in possession of land less than his share is always entitled to pray for partition by brining a suit in a Court of competent jurisdiction and if his claim is proved he is entitled to get land partitioned through Court. A co-sharer in possession of excess land than his share is bound to part with the same."</u>
<u>9. In this case, as per the evidence of plaintiffs and defendants we find that Sahachari and Gayashwari got life estate in the suit land and after their demise the 3(three) sons of Sahachari namely Kiron, Dinesh and Haripada and one son of Gayashwari namely Ashwani would get equal share in the suit land as grandsons of late Dinu Mondal. Although, in the record we find that defendant Ashwani son of Gayashwari had owned has been owning and possessing more than the share he is entitle to and he has transferred more than his 4 annas share which he is bound to part with as per the decision reported in 12 MLR (AD) 347. The submission of Mr Bhowmick that the son of Sahachari admitted the title of Ashwani to the extent of 8 annas share of the suit land by purchase from him each plots and now their sons or grandsons cannot disown the title of the defendant cannot be accepted because principle of estopple does not lie against law. The property shall be devolved upon the Dinus grandson as per Hindu Dayabhaga System per capita. The submission of Mr Bhowmick that the heirs of Sahachari and Gayashwari will receive the property left by them per stripes is not correct because Sahachari and Gayashwari enjoyed and got the suit property as life estate and therefore, the main heirs of Dinu Mondal being the sons of his 2(two) daughters will get the suit property per-capita i.e., Kiron, Dinesh, Haripada and Ashwani each will get 4 annas share of the suit property and the present plaintiff being the heirs of Kiron, Dinesh and Haripada will get 12 arenas of the total property left by Dukhi Bewa and one son of Gayashwari namely Ashwani will get 4 annas of the total land. The trial Court on correct assessment of fact and law, considering the Dayabhaga System of the Hindu Law decreed the suit finding plaintiffs' title and ejmali possession over the suit land.</u>
10. We find nothing wrong in the impugned judgment and decree, therefore, we find no merit in this appeal. Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs. The judgment and decree passed by the trial Court is hereby affirmed.
Communicate the judgment and send down the lower Court records.
End.

VS
